# GMRI | Thirty-Day Human-Life Threat Assessment

*Operational intelligence edition: evidence before exposure, not casualty counts after the fact*

**Version 6 | Issued November 3, 2026 | Forecast interval November 3–December 3, 2026**  
**Primary scope:** Civilian safety in the United States; domestic military missions, federal coercive operations, emergency medical access, continuity of essential services. **Regional attention:** Western states and Texas without assuming a particular county is the target.  
**Evidence cutoff:** Public material available November 3, 2026. All forecasts are analyst judgments, not intercepted orders or reports of secret plans.

## Executive assessment

**Main forecast:** For the next 30 days, the most evidence-supported operational pattern is the **continuation of dispersed federal immigration enforcement**, including short-notice, small-team activity in jurisdictions already affected by the October California surge. Additional civilian encounters and the possibility of injury are credible consequences. The stronger forecast is that the **existing enforcement tempo persists**, not that a particular location or person will be attacked. [R05–R08, R28–R30]

**High-consequence alternative:** A **localized domestic military-support mission** could be ordered on short notice under already established Guard response arrangements. The October 2025 National Guard Bureau directive specifies an eight-hour initial-response standard and 24-hour full-response standard for its designated force; it does **not** demonstrate that every unit is currently ready or that an activation is pending. The decisive missing record is **current mission tasking and command transfer**, not statutory permission. [R01–R02, R23, R31]

**Critical revision to the model:** A court found that troops **had already** been used to enforce civilian law in Los Angeles in 2025, in violation of the Posse Comitatus Act. That finding was issued **after** the deployment. Legality is therefore **not counted as an advance safety barrier**. Judicial rulings remain relevant to later conduct and institutional resistance, but only observed compliance—not a paper prohibition—can reduce the forecast of exposure. [R03, R32]

**Medical-response warning:** Prior independently investigated federal action included projectiles directed at identifiable volunteer medics and chemical irritants deployed into treatment tents. The mechanism to watch **before someone is injured** is restricted patient access, an impending operation near a treatment location, or a documented command decision permitting force near medical services—not whether a responder recognizes a threat while caring for a patient. [R10–R11]

**What is *not* substantiated:** As of the evidence cutoff, this review found **no authenticated new order** directing nationwide deployment of the National Guard quick-reaction force, replacing civilian government across the country, or targeting a particular family or city. This is a limited statement about the records examined, **not** an assumption that an illegal act will be announced in advance, nor a guarantee that it cannot occur.

## 1. The operational pattern the previous editions missed

The case study is not the court's declaration that unlawful policing occurred. The **sequence** matters:

| When | Decision or observation | Why it matters for prediction |
|---|---|---|
| June 2025 | The administration deployed California National Guard members and Marines in Los Angeles amid federal enforcement and protests. | Military action reached civilian streets **before** final judicial findings. [R32] |
| September 2, 2025 | The district court found that military personnel had performed civilian law-enforcement functions in violation of the Posse Comitatus Act. Its judgment records crowd control, protective perimeters and traffic blockades. | A legal restriction failed to prevent the initial exposure. The court later provided an accountability mechanism; it was not an operational warning system. [R32] |
| August 25–October 31, 2025 | Executive Order 14339 and the National Guard Bureau memorandum established a nationwide quick-reaction training and readiness program for civil-disturbance missions. | Standing **capability**, not a November 2026 activation indicator. [R01, R31] |
| Through 2026 | National Guard personnel remained assigned to civilian security in Washington, D.C.; NPR reported temporary Marshals Service deputization allowing detention but not arrest. | Military–civilian authority was being exercised, not merely proposed; D.C. does not establish authority elsewhere. [R25] |
| October 5–9, 2026 | California Central Valley enforcement surge began; local reporting documented operations and community effects by October 9. | **Field reporting preceded** wider confirmation of internal planning. [R29–R30] |
| October 23, 2026 | Ninth Circuit affirmed an injunction concerning the earlier California Guard federalization. | A meaningful constraint on one deployment pathway; **not evidence that executives cannot try another route**. [R03] |
| October 31, 2026 | Reuters reported an internal email describing the Central Valley operation planned in early October and executed by smaller teams moving among towns. | A deployment can be underway **weeks before** a nationally prominent report confirms its internal direction. [R06, R28] |

**Derived signal:** There is a roughly **22-day interval** between the October 9 local investigative account and the October 31 Reuters report examining internal operational communication. It is *not* a measured average warning lead time. It demonstrates why national confirmation is an unsuitable prerequisite for recognizing activity that local observers can already substantiate. [R28, R30]

**Analytic consequence:** Replace the prior model—*Is a deployment allowed? Has anybody publicly announced it?*—with: *What force exists? What is it currently tasked to do? Which local observations confirm execution? What change would expose civilians and responders next?*

## 2. The forecast register: propositions that can be marked right or wrong

These are **dated forward propositions**, not probability estimates manufactured from sparse incidents. Confidence measures the strength of the evidence supporting the direction of the forecast; it does not state a mathematical probability of harm.

| ID / deadline | Forecast | Confidence and basis | What would falsify or materially revise it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **F1 / Nov 10** | **Dispersed immigration enforcement continues in the California Central Valley** beyond November 3, with independently documented field activity or new detentions. | **Moderate–high.** Active October operation, local corroboration, internal email reviewed by Reuters. [R06, R28–R30] | Corroborated stand-down, cessation across affected jurisdictions, or a clearly superseding directive. |
| **F2 / Dec 3** | **Federal enforcement continues through geographically distributed, relatively small operations**, rather than requiring a fresh, highly publicized large-city deployment. | **Moderate.** October regional pattern plus expanding local agreements. [R05–R08] | Documented material stand-down across several regions and replacement of dispersed operations by a substantially different operating pattern. |
| **F3 / Dec 3** | **Further serious civilian-force encounters are plausible** during ongoing operations; specific injuries, persons, and dates cannot be confidently forecast from the available denominator. | **Moderate for exposure; low for precise injury prediction.** Past incidents establish a failure mode; current operations create additional contact opportunities. [R09–R11, R28] | Verified sustained reduction in force per comparable encounter plus transparent, complete incident reporting. |
| **F4 / Dec 3** | **A new localized Guard support mission is a credible contingency**, but not the baseline prediction; a synchronized nationwide activation is not supported by current public tasking evidence. | **Low–moderate for occurrence, high consequence.** Standing readiness directive, previously exercised missions, and known mobilization precedent. [R01–R03, R23–R25, R32] | Authenticated activation/tasking raises concern immediately; verified demobilization and concrete limits on mission assignment lower it. |
| **F5 / Dec 3** | **An additional medical-access obstruction is a credible operational hazard** where enforcement and public gatherings coincide; no specific next attack on a medic is established. | **Moderate for failure mode; low for site/timing.** Independent investigation documents prior obstruction while treatment was underway. [R10] | Credible, observed improvements in scene access and pre-established access procedures sustained across operations. |
| **F6 / Dec 3** | **Water-sector disruptions may recur locally**; there is no substantiated bridge linking those incidents to domestic security operations. | **Moderate for recurring vulnerability; low for where/when.** FBI/EPA documented actual July disruption. [R14–R15] | Confirmed remediation and no continuing intrusions in adequately observed systems lower risk; shared operational evidence would be needed for attribution or coordination. |
| **F7 / Dec 3** | **Implemented health-coverage restrictions continue generating payer/provider adjustments**, with possible care interruption for people relying on affected coverage. | **High for administrative implementation; unquantified for health harm.** October federal effective date and November 2 state bulletin. [R16–R17] | Controlling injunction, replacement rule or corrected claims policy. |

**The forecast I do *not* make:** “Nationwide martial law begins on [invented date].” The presence of an available force, prior unlawful conduct, and political language cannot establish an exact operation or date. Neither should the lack of that proof be treated as evidence of safety.

## 3. A warning system that looks upstream of casualties

**Event sequence:** Political or administrative intent → resources and standing capability → **specific tasking / interagency mission assignment** → observable deployment and changes to civilian services → civilian exposure → injury/death → investigation.

The earlier reports placed too much weight on the right-hand side. A usable warning must give primacy to **tasking and observable deployment**.

| Alert condition | What qualifies as evidence | What it means / appropriate nonviolent response |
|---|---|---|
| **Baseline capacity** | Executive order, readiness target, procurement or a standing training cycle, without new orders. | Long-horizon capability. **Do not** describe it as proof of a present attack or counsel evacuation on this alone. |
| **Operational change** | Dated authenticated tasking, unit assignment, a newly announced federal-local operation, or separately corroborated enforcement activity in a defined locality. | Update affected-area advisories and operational continuity plans; identify the agencies and their actual mission, not just their uniforms. |
| **Civilian exposure** | Credible reports of a new checkpoint, movement restriction, direct interference with ambulances, medical tents, clinics, or emergency communications. | **Immediate locality-specific safety concern.** Medical leadership should invoke prearranged access escalation, mutual-aid and reporting procedures rather than relying on individual responders to improvise under fire. |
| **Systemwide escalation** | Concurrent authenticated military assignments to ordinary civilian police functions in **multiple** jurisdictions, plus effective displacement of civilian command or institutions. | Reclassify the national threat assessment urgently. An event does not require a public declaration to satisfy this evidence test. |

**Two independent confirmations** should be preferred for unsourced claims of deployments, but **a single authenticated operational document or directly verified active threat** is sufficient to justify urgent safety action. The evidentiary standard is calibrated to the speed and consequence of the event; it is not a procedural excuse for waiting.

### The activation question, stripped of legalism

The **National Guard Quick Reaction Force (NGQRF)** memorandum specified a 200-person CASE-associated mission element, 25% prepared within eight hours, 50% within twelve, and 100% within twenty-four; it also requires monthly readiness reporting by the twentieth. This is a **force design and readiness requirement**—not proof of achieved readiness, a new 2026 order, or a standardized 200-person force in every county. The **National Guard Reaction Force (NGRF)** is a distinct older construct. [R01, R23]

For a 30-day warning, the important missing pieces are: **current unit status; a real mission assignment; the receiving civilian agency; the command and operational control actually exercised; and the location where personnel will perform functions affecting civilians.** Senators Kelly and Slotkin sought those items in October, including possible DHS and DOJ support. The signed letter requests response by October 29, though its press summary says October 28. [R02, R26]

**Operational safeguard—not legal assumption:** The October 23 California appellate judgment and 2026 demobilizations are counterevidence against continuous occupation of the earlier locations. They do not prove that another commander will comply in the next incident. [R03, R24]

## 4. The medical danger: why “scene safety” is the wrong after-the-fact answer

Human Rights Watch documented federal agents firing projectiles at identifiable volunteer medics, impeding treatment and evacuation, and deploying chemical irritants into two medical tents at Broadview in September 2025. A medic reported an agent firing at him while he was kneeling to treat an injured person. These are **observed failure modes**, not forecasts of a scheduled attack in November 2026. [R10]

**There is no meaningful individual threat assessment once care is underway and force arrives without warning.** The useful intelligence must reach dispatch, medical command and health facilities **before** that collision occurs. The institution-level indicators are a new operation affecting access routes to care; repeated force where medics are working; prior inability to contact an accountable scene commander; and credible restrictions on patient transport or emergency dispatch.

**Protective decision:** Medical organizations can establish independent ambulance-access and escalation contacts, secondary communications, documentation of impeded care, and mutual-aid arrangements *before* major enforcement activity. These are non-confrontational continuity controls; they do not make live fire predictable or safe for the clinician.

The GAO found ICE lacked controls to ensure mandatory body-camera activation. Consequently, missing video cannot be used as negative evidence that an encounter did not occur. It also means independent contemporaneous records can be indispensable. [R11]

## 5. Correlated patterns are not automatically a common operation

This report considers five interacting systems: **federal operational leadership, National Guard capacity, immigration-enforcement partnerships, medical-response access, and local water/communications infrastructure**. Each has a separate evidence chain.

- **Joint command or shared operational tasking** would link military personnel with a federal civilian action. Coincident headlines do not.
- **An authenticated order changing medical access** would link a security operation to a care interruption. A later injury alone cannot tell us the advance decision.
- **Shared technical telemetry, contractor or command records** would be required to connect infrastructure disruptions to a security action. The July FBI/EPA water advisory establishes a cyber hazard, **not** a common conspiracy. [R14–R15]
- **Policy-to-action continuity** is independently demonstrable: Project 2025 proposed changes; later executive and agency instruments altered specific federal protections and reimbursement arrangements. Those are real administrative changes, but do not alone establish a planned lethal campaign. [R16–R21]

The strongest pattern is **capability plus a demonstrated willingness to use it**, with local reports serving as the earliest publicly available operational confirmations. That pattern increases the need for vigilance; it does not disclose an unobserved target or date.

## 6. Conditions that should change a real-world decision

### Next 72 hours (November 3–6)

**Current classification: standing strategic concern; locality-specific operational concern where activity is independently documented.** The strongest contemporary field receipt is the California Central Valley operation, not a universal national activation. Confirm changes in actual regional deployments and restrictions on civilian or medical movement rather than recycling last year's force-creation order. [R28–R30]

**Escalate immediately if** a dated Guard or military assignment to civilian enforcement is verified, if medical access is physically obstructed, or if a directly verified threat identifies a specific location. The existence of a new court filing without an implemented order does not by itself establish exposure.

### November 7–17

Test F1 and F2 against local verified enforcement reporting. If new deployments move beyond the known California pattern, document **who, where, when, mission and civilian effect**; a dramatic label without these elements is not actionable. Verify any newly released NGQRF readiness or congressional-response material for **tasking**, not merely staffing.

### November 18–December 3

The November 20 readiness-report deadline is a **scheduled internal reporting point**, not a predicted day of deployment. Escalate any observed change in unit mission or police power promptly. Review repeated impediments to care, field use-of-force, documented regional detention changes, and new utility service notices. Revise the entire hypothesis if a shared command/resourcing link emerges across systems. [R01]

### Practical safety implication

For a specific person or household, the evidence in this report **does not support an order to flee, a prediction of a targeted attack, or a claim that any community is safe by virtue of court orders**. An immediate decision should be driven by a **credible local threat, active restriction of movement or medical access, or authoritative emergency information**, not by a generic national mood estimate.

## 7. Disconfirming evidence the analysis must keep

**Do not cherry-pick toward catastrophe.** The October 23 Ninth Circuit ruling affirmed a substantial constraint on the earlier California federalization; NORTHCOM reported demobilizations in locations previously under federal protection missions. A Defense Department response said no troops were planned for polling sites, a claim about one mission rather than all future deployment. These facts reduce support for specific scenarios, even while the Los Angeles record shows why legality itself cannot be a reliable safety screen. [R03–R04, R24, R32]

**Do not cherry-pick toward reassurance.** The fact that a court rules later does not reverse earlier exposure; the fact that a force is officially intended for rapid reaction does not prove that it is inactive; the absence of a visible document may reflect nonpublic records rather than absence of action. Do not promote any of those absences into a positive safety claim.

**Separate the scenarios:** (H1) continued dispersed federal enforcement; (H2) localized military support to a civilian mission; (H3) coordinated displacement of civilian governance across jurisdictions; (H4) an unrelated infrastructure event; (H5) distinct health-policy implementation effects. No single hidden-operation explanation currently links all five.

## 8. The evidence that is still missing

| Missing item | Why it matters | What *would* count |
|---|---|---|
| Current November NGQRF/NGRF tasking and readiness | Converts a standing capability into an assessed mission | Authenticated dated activation/tasking and current operational status; monthly DRRS report if publicly available. |
| Reply, if any, to the October Senate Guard inquiry | Might clarify if support to DHS/DOJ was contemplated | Signed DoD/NGB response; a missing public reply alone is not evidence of concealment. |
| New regional agency notifications | Can precede widely reported enforcement operations | Dated field instructions or corroborated local reporting; no guessed targets. |
| Local medical-access notifications and incident logs | Earlier than or independent of a casualty count | EMS/hospital warnings, documented ambulance delays, direct verified interference. |
| Accurate use-of-force denominators and recording compliance | Needed for rates and calibrated casualty probabilities | Comparable encounter totals, incident definitions, independently auditable footage/records. |
| Cross-system link evidence | Needed before alleging coordinated hostile action | Shared authenticated orders, responsible officials, funding or technical telemetry. |

## 9. Forecast accountability and evidence rules

A forecast can be **confirmed**, **disconfirmed**, or **unresolved** at its deadline. An event that happens after an unfounded prediction does not retroactively justify fabricated evidence or a false assertion of prior knowledge. Neither does a court's subsequent ruling erase an unlawful earlier operation. A new warning **requires a new observation**, not a more emotional description of an existing fact.

**Evidence classifications:** *Verified* means a primary source or source document was inspected; *Reported* means independently attributed field reporting; *Calculated* means transparent arithmetic from grounded dates; *Inferred* means an explicitly stated judgment about a possible next step; *Unresolved* means the necessary source was not accessible. Sources are cited in the receipt ledger below. The report contains no invented classified access or unsupported family-specific threat information.

**What this edition changes:** It replaces reliance on statutory prohibition with empirical compliance, puts current tasking ahead of standing readiness, uses the Central Valley reporting sequence as a real early-warning case study, separates medics' safety from the unrealistic demand for individual anticipation under fire, and exposes its forecasts to a dated outcome check.

# PDF Skill (Read • Inspect • Extract • Edit • Render • Forms • OCR • Redact • Convert • Diff)

This skill is designed for **reliable, workflow-driven** PDF work: **render -> verify -> operate -> re-render verify**.

## Before you touch PDFs: should this be DOCX/PPTX instead?

Even if the user asks for a PDF deliverable, the best workflow is often:

- **Text-heavy, business-doc layout (headings, TOC, long tables, rich lists)** -> use the **DOCX skill** to author, then convert to PDF with `lo_convert_to_pdf.py`.
- **Slide-like visual layout (charts, callouts, fixed positioning, figure captions)** -> use the **Slides skill** (PPTX) to author, then export to PDF.
- **Programmatic generation** -> ReportLab (this skill) is fine.

If you find yourself hand-tuning line breaks or typography in ReportLab, you probably picked the wrong authoring format.

## Core loop (always)

1) Render to images

```bash
python /home/oai/skills/pdfs/scripts/render_pdf.py input.pdf --out_dir /mnt/data/_renders/in --dpi 200
```

2) Inspect PNGs (tables/figures/layout are authoritative)

3) Perform the edit/extract/create

4) Re-render and compare

```bash
python /home/oai/skills/pdfs/scripts/compare_renders.py before.pdf after.pdf --out_dir /mnt/data/_diff --dpi 200
```

## Design standards for document generation

For generating new documents or major rewrite/repackages, follow the design standards below unless the user explicitly requests otherwise. The user's instructions always take precedence; otherwise, adhere to these standards.

When creating the document design, do not compromise on the content and make factual/technical errors. Do not produce something that looks polished but not actually what the user requested.

It is very important that the document is professional and aesthetically pleasing. As such, you should follow this general workflow to make your final delivered document:

1. Before you make the PDF, please first think about the high-level design of the PDF:
   - Before creating the document, decide what kind of document it is (for example, a memo, report, SOP, workflow, form, proposal, or manual) and design accordingly. In general, you shall create documents which are professional, visually polished, and aesthetically pleasing. However, you should also calibrate the level of styling to the document's purpose: for formal, serious, or highly utilitarian documents, visual appeal should come mainly from strong typography, spacing, hierarchy, and overall polish rather than expressive styling. The goal is for the document's visual character to feel appropriate to its real-world use case, with readability and usability always taking priority.
   - You should make documents that feel visually natural. If a human looks at your document, they should find the design natural and smooth. This is very important; please think carefully about how to achieve this.
   - Think about how you would like the first page to be organized. How about subsequent pages? What about the placement of the title? What does the heading ladder look like? Should there be a clear hierarchy? etc
   - Would you like to include visual components, such as tables, callouts, checklists, images, etc? If yes, then plan out the design for each component.
   - Think about the general spacing and layout. What will be the default body spacing? What page budget is allocated between packaging and substance? How will page breaks behave around tables and figures, since we must make sure to avoid large blank gaps, keep captions and their visuals together when possible, and keep content from becoming too wide by maintaining generous side margins so the page feels balanced and natural.
   - Think about font, type scale, consistent accent treatment, etc. Try to avoid forcing large chunks of small text into narrow areas. When space is tight, adjust font size, line breaks, alignment, or layout instead of cramming in more text.
2. Once you have a working PDF, continue iterating until the entire document is polished and correct. After every change or edit, render the PDF and review it carefully to evaluate the result. The plan from (1) should guide you, but it is only a flexible draft; you should update your decisions as needed throughout the revision process. Important: each time you render and reflect, you should check for both:
   1. Design aesthetics: the document should be aesthetically pleasing and easy to skim. Ask yourself: if a human were to look at my document, would they find it aesthetically nice? It should feel natural, smooth, and visually cohesive.
   2. Formatting issues that need to be fixed: e.g. text overlap, overflow, cramped spacing between adjacent elements, awkward spacing in tables/charts, awkward page breaks, etc. This is super important. Do not stop revising until all formatting issues are fixed.

While making and revising the PDF, please adhere to and check against these quality reminders, to ensure the deliverable is visually high quality:

- Document density: Try to avoid having verbose dense walls of text, unless it's necessary. Avoid long runs of consecutive plain paragraphs or too many words before visual anchors. For some tasks this may be necessary (i.e. verbose legal documents); in those cases ignore this suggestion.
- Font: Use professional, easy-to-read font choices with appropriate size that is not too small. Usage of bold, underlines, and italics should be professional.
- Color: Use color intentionally for titles, headings, subheadings, and selective emphasis so important information stands out in a visually appealing way. The palette and intensity should fit the document's purpose, with more restrained use where a formal or serious tone is needed.
- Visuals: Consider using tables, diagrams, and other visual components when they improve comprehension, navigation, or usability.
- Tables: Please invest significant effort to make sure your tables are well-made and aesthetically/visually good. Below are some suggestions, as well as some hard constraints that you must relentlessly check to make sure your table satisfies them.
  - Suggestions:
    - Set deliberate table/cell widths and heights instead of defaulting to full page width.
    - Choose column widths intentionally rather than giving every column equal width by default. Very short fields (for example: item number, checkbox, score, result, year, date, or status) should usually be kept compact, while wider columns should be reserved for longer content.
    - Avoid overly wide tables, and leave generous side margins so the layout feels natural.
    - Keep all text vertically centered and make deliberate horizontal alignment choices.
    - Ensure cell height avoids a crowded look. Leave clear vertical spacing between a table and its caption or following text.
  - Hard constraints:
    - To prevent clipping/overflow:
      - Never use fixed row heights that can truncate text; allow rows to expand with wrapped content.
      - Ensure cell padding and line spacing are sufficient so descenders/ascenders don't get clipped.
      - If content is tight, prefer (in order): wrap text -> adjust column widths -> reduce font slightly -> abbreviate headers/use two-line headers.
    - Padding / breathing room: Ensure text doesn't sit against cell borders or look "pinned" to the upper-left. Favor generous internal padding on all sides, and keep it consistent across the table.
    - Vertical alignment: In general, you should center your text vertically. Make sure that the content uses the available cell space naturally rather than clustering at the top.
    - Horizontal alignment: Do not default all body cells to top-left alignment. Choose horizontal alignment intentionally by column type: centered alignment often works best for short values, status fields, dates, numbers, and check indicators; left alignment is usually better for narrative or multi-line text.
    - Line height inside cells: Use line spacing that avoids a cramped feel and prevents ascenders/descenders from looking clipped. If a cell feels tight, adjust wrapping/width/padding before shrinking type.
    - Width + wrapping sanity check: Avoid default equal-width columns when the content in each column clearly has different sizes. Avoid lines that run so close to the right edge that the cell feels overfull. If this happens, prefer wrapping or column-width adjustments before reducing font size.
    - Spacing around tables: Keep clear separation between tables and surrounding text (especially the paragraph immediately above/below) so the layout doesn't feel stuck together. Captions and tables should stay visually paired, with deliberate spacing.
    - Quick visual QA pass: Look for text that appears "boundary-hugging", specifically content pressed against the top or left edge of a cell or sitting too close beneath a table. Also watch for overly narrow descriptive columns and short-value columns whose contents feel awkwardly pinned. Correct these issues through padding, alignment, wrapping, or small column-width adjustments.
- Forms / questionnaires: Design these as a usable form, not a spreadsheet.
  - Prioritize clear response options, obvious and well-sized check targets, readable scale labels, generous row height, clear section hierarchy, light visual structure. Please size fields and columns based on the content they hold rather than by equal-width table cells.
  - Use spacing, alignment, and subtle header/section styling to organize the page. Avoid dense full-grid borders, cramped layouts, and ambiguous numeric-only response areas.
- Coherence vs. fragmentation: In general, try to keep things to be one coherent representation rather than fragmented, if possible.
  - For example, don't split one logical dataset across multiple independent tables unless there's a clear, labeled reason.
  - For example, if a table must span across pages, continue to the next page with a repeated header and consistent column order
- Background shapes/colors: Where helpful, consider section bands, note boxes, control grids, or other visual containers with suitable colors to improve scanability and communication. Use them when they suit the document type. If you do use these, make sure they are formatted well, with no overlaps, awkward spacing, etc.
- Spacing: Please check rigorously for spacing issues. Please always use a natural amount of spacing between adjacent components. Use clear, generous vertical spacing between sections and paragraphs, and leave a bit of extra space between subheadings and the content that follows when it improves readability. Use indentation and alignment intentionally so the document's hierarchy is immediately clear. At the same time, avoid large "layout gaps" caused by a table or chart not fitting at the bottom of a page and getting pushed to the next one. If this happens, please try these suggestions:
  - moving the preceding paragraph(s) with it to the next page to keep the narrative cohesive
  - scaling the visual modestly or simplify labels without hurting readability, formatting, or aesthetics of the visual
  - Splitting the table/figure cleanly across multiple pages, but use repeated headers to make the page continuation clear.
- Text boxes: For text boxes, please follow the same breathing-room rules as the tables: make sure to use generous internal padding, intentional alignment, and sufficient line spacing so text never feels cramped, clipped, or pinned to the edges. Keep spacing around the text box clear so it remains visually distinct from surrounding content, and if the content feels tight, prefer adjusting box size, padding, or text wrapping before reducing font size.
- Layout/archetype: Remember to choose the right document archetype/template (proposal, SOP, workflow, form, handbook, etc.). Use a coherent style system. Once a style system is chosen, apply it consistently across headings, spacing, table treatments, callouts, and accent usage. If appropriate to the document type, include a cover page or front-matter elements such as title, subtitle, metadata, or branding.

## Package map (where things live)

This pack includes a `manifest.txt` that is a **pure list of relative file paths** used by download tooling.

Quick map:

- **tasks/** (what to do)
  - `read_review.md` - render-first reading/review
  - `extract.md` - extract text/layout/tables/images/attachments/forms
  - `coords.md` - coordinate system cheatsheet (PDF pt vs image px)
  - `edit.md` - merge/split/select/rotate/crop/watermark/paginate/encrypt/repair
  - `compare.md` - visual diff workflow
  - `forms_annotations.md` - fillable forms + appearance pitfalls + correctness checklist
  - `forms_debugging.md` - widget-level introspection + acceptable values
  - `forms_nonfillable.md` - stamp-by-boxes workflow for non-fillable forms
  - `ocr.md` - OCR scanned PDFs to searchable
  - `preflight.md` - quick triage + normalization guidance
  - `redact.md` - true redaction workflows
  - `parity.md` - render parity across engines
  - `batch.md` - batch helpers for corpora
  - `create.md` - choose reportlab/latex/html/docx/pptx pipeline
  - `convert.md` - docx/pptx/html/markdown/latex to PDF conversion
  - `js_tools.md` - pdf-lib/pdfjs helper CLIs

- **scripts/** (run these)
  - `render_pdf.py` - render to PNGs (pdfium or poppler)
  - `compare_renders.py` - render-and-diff two PDFs (pixel diff)
  - `pdf_inspect.py` - metadata/structure overview
  - `pdf_extract.py` - text/words/chars/tables/images/attachments/annots/forms
  - `pdf_edit.py` - editing toolkit (merge/split/select/rotate/crop/watermark/paginate/encrypt/repair/optimize)
  - `pdf_preflight.py` - preflight/triage warnings
  - `pdf_redact.py` - true redaction (remove underlying content)
  - `renderer_parity.py` - diff pdftoppm vs pdfium renders
  - `batch_pdf.py` - batch runner for common ops
  - `box_picker_html.py` - generate interactive HTML to pick rectangles -> JSON in PDF coords
  - `place_text_by_boxes.py` - stamp text/checkmarks into rectangles (non-fillable forms)
  - `ocr_pdf.py` - OCR wrapper
  - `html_to_pdf.py`, `md_to_pdf.py`, `latex_to_pdf.py`, `lo_convert_to_pdf.py` - conversion helpers

- **js/** (Node helpers)
  - `install_deps.sh` - installs pdf-lib + pdfjs-dist
  - `fill_form.mjs` - fill + optional flatten (supports flags and positional args)
  - `extract_form_fields.mjs` - list AcroForm fields
  - `extract_text_pdfjs.mjs` - extract text via pdfjs-dist

- **examples/**
  - `smoke_test.md` - runnable smoke flows

- **troubleshooting/**
  - `common.md` - common pitfalls and fixes

## Final deliverable expectations

- No clipped text, overlaps, black squares, or broken glyphs in rendered PNGs.
- Verify in at least **one** renderer (`pdfium` or `pdftoppm`). For tricky forms, verify in **two**.
- Remove intermediate artifacts from the deliverable folder (keep only final PDF(s)).
- Avoid Unicode dashes that some renderers mishandle; prefer ASCII `-`.

                                      A.

[L146]     Olmstead involved the claims of two “mentally retarded women,” one
[L147] of whom “ha[d] also been diagnosed with schizophrenia,” the other “with
[L148] a personality disorder.” Id. at 593. Each was confined to a psychiatric
[L149] facility in Georgia during an episode of acute illness. Id. Both alleged,
[L150] inter alia, that Georgia healthcare officials had violated Title II by keep-
[L151] ing them confined in the institution after “treating professionals deter-
[L152] mined” that placement in “a community-based program” was appropriate.
[L153] Id. at 594. When their case reached the Supreme Court, the question
[L154] presented was “whether the [ADA’s] proscription of discrimination may
[L155] require placement of persons with mental disabilities in community set-
[L156] tings rather than in institutions.” Id. at 587 (plurality opinion). A plurality
[L157] of the Court answered that question with “a qualified yes.” Id.
[L158]     The Court—by the narrowest possible margin—held that “unjustified
[L159] institutional isolation of persons with disabilities is a form of discrimina-
[L160] tion” prohibited under Title II. Id. at 600 (majority opinion). It drew this
[L161] conclusion not from the ADA’s text but by reference to DOJ’s regula-
[L162] tions. See id. at 596–603. Specifically, the Court took 28 C.F.R.
[L163] § 35.130(d) as its starting point, noting that “the Attorney General con-
[L164] cluded that unjustified placement or retention of persons in institutions
[L165] . . . constitutes a form of discrimination based on disability.” Id. at 596.
[L166] Because DOJ is “the agency directed by Congress to issue regulations
[L167] implementing Title II,” the Court concluded that the department’s view
[L168] “warrant[ed] respect.” Id. at 597–98. But the Court also emphasized
[L169] that its opinion did not “determine the[] validity” of any such regulation.
[L170] Id. at 592.
[L171]     In seeking to persuade the Court to the contrary, Georgia had made two
[L172] counterarguments rooted in Title II’s text. The State argued that institu-
[L173] tional isolation of individuals with mental disabilities cannot be “discrim-
[L174] ination ‘by reason of’ . . . disabilities” when patients are “not denied
[L175] community placement on account of those disabilities” but on account of
[L176] other factors. Id. at 598 (emphasis added) (citation omitted). Nor could it
[L177] be discrimination, said the State, because “‘discrimination’ necessarily
[L178] requires uneven treatment of similarly situated individuals.” Id. (citation
[L179] omitted).


                                       4
[L184] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 5 / 39>[L185] Whether the Rehabilitation Act or ADA Impose or Authorize an Integration Mandate

[L187]    The Court rebuffed those arguments, writing that “Congress had a more
[L188] comprehensive view of the concept of discrimination advanced in the
[L189] ADA” than the statutory text suggested—a view that encompassed unjus-
[L190] tified institutional isolation, even without a similarly situated comparator.
[L191] Id. at 598 & n.10; see id. at 598–600. As support for this conclusion, the
[L192] Court pointed to (1) Congress’s general efforts “to secure opportunities
[L193] for people with developmental disabilities to enjoy the benefits of com-
[L194] munity living,” and (2) Congress’s “findings” underlying the ADA, which
[L195] twice identified “segregation” as a “for[m] of discrimination.” Id. at 599–
[L196] 600 (alteration in original) (quoting 42 U.S.C. § 12101(a)(2), (5)). Then,
[L197] hypothesizing why Congress may have considered unjustified isolation to
[L198] be discriminatory, the Court observed that isolation does create
[L199] “[d]issimilar treatment,” in that it requires “persons with mental disabili-
[L200] ties . . . [to] relinquish participation in community life they could enjoy
[L201] given reasonable accommodations” in order to receive medical services,
[L202] “while persons without mental disabilities can receive the medical ser-
[L203] vices they need without similar sacrifice.” Id. at 601.6
[L204]    Importantly for the purpose of your question, although a majority of the
[L205] Court agreed that Title II prohibited “unjustified institutional isolation,”
[L206] id. at 600, that majority splintered in suggesting how to determine when
[L207] “States are required to provide community-based treatment for persons
[L208] with mental disabilities,” id. at 607 (plurality opinion). Justice Ginsburg,
[L209] writing for a plurality of four, instructed lower courts to consider whether:
[L210] (1) “the State’s treatment professionals determine that such placement is
[L211] appropriate,” (2) “the affected persons do not oppose such treatment,”
[L212] and (3) “the placement can be reasonably accommodated, taking into
[L213] account the resources available to the State and the needs of others with
[L214] mental disabilities.” Id. In a portion of the opinion belonging to the plural-
[L215] ity, Justice Ginsburg stated that when all three conditions attain, deinstitu-
[L216] tionalization is mandatory. See id.; see also id. at 587 (asserting that
[L217] community-based treatment “is in order” under these conditions).

[L219]    6 In doing so, the Court did not expressly distinguish between the named plaintiffs’

[L221] developmental disabilities and the acute episodes of mental illness that led to their
[L222] institutionalization—instead referring only to “mental disability.” E.g., Olmstead, 527
[L223] U.S. at 597–603 (majority opinion). This treatment is consistent with other instances
[L224] in which the law has treated mental illness and disability as synonymous. See, e.g.,
[L225] Schweiker v. Wilson, 450 U.S. 221, 231–32 n.14 (1981). Given that those distinctions do
[L226] not affect our analysis, we will follow the convention set by Olmstead.

[L230] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 6 / 39>[L231]                            50 Op. O.L.C. __ (June 18, 2026)

[L233]    The case generated three additional opinions. First, Justice Stevens
[L234] concurred in the judgment as well as in the majority’s fundamental hold-
[L235] ing that “‘unjustified institutional isolation[]’ constitutes discrimination
[L236] under the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990.” Id. at 607 (Stevens,
[L237] J., concurring in part and concurring in the judgment). He withheld his
[L238] vote, however, from the plurality’s definition of when isolation is unjusti-
[L239] fied. Id. at 607–08. Instead, he would have remanded for the district court
[L240] to consider that question in the first instance. Id.
[L241]    Second, Justice Kennedy concurred in the Court’s judgment but not its
[L242] reasoning, writing separately both to express reservations and to explain
[L243] how unjustified institutional isolation may constitute unlawful discrimina-
[L244] tion. Id. at 609–12 (Kennedy, J., concurring in the judgment). His reserva-
[L245] tions—shared by Justice Breyer—grew out of the “dark side” of deinstitu-
[L246] tionalization. Id. at 609. Justice Kennedy observed that patients pre-
[L247] maturely released from in-patient care frequently end up homeless or even
[L248] incarcerated. Id. at 609–10. In words that have proven all too prescient, 7
[L249] he remarked “it would be a tragic event . . . were the [ADA] to be inter-
[L250] preted so that States had some incentive, for fear of litigation, to drive
[L251] those in need of medical care and treatment out of appropriate care and
[L252] into settings with too little assistance and supervision.” Id. at 610. Justice
[L253] Kennedy therefore advised “caution and circumspection” in
[L254] holding States liable for institutionalizing patients, along with “great
[L255] deference to the medical decisions of the responsible, treating physicians”
[L256] and “appropriate deference to the program funding decisions of state
[L257] policymakers.” Id.
[L258]    As for the discriminatory nature of institutional isolation, Justice Ken-
[L259] nedy (writing only for himself) accepted the dissent’s view that “the
[L260] ordinary interpretation and meaning” of the term “discrimination” neces-
[L261] sarily implies “differential treatment vis-à-vis members of a different
[L262] group on the basis of a statutorily described characteristic.” Id. at 611

[L264]     7 In just the period between 2018 and 2024, the rate of chronic homelessness increased

[L266] by over 70%. Akash Pillai, Heather Saunders & Robin Rudowitz, Five Key Facts About
[L267] People Experiencing Homelessness, Kaiser Family Found. (Sept. 9, 2025), https://
[L268] perma.cc/KJ3F-WC87. Of the individuals experiencing homelessness in 2024, 22% had
[L269] serious mental illness, id., and 67% had some mental-health disorder, Rebecca Barry et
[L270] al., Prevalence of Mental Health Disorders Among Individuals Experiencing Homeless-
[L271] ness: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis, 81 JAMA Psychiatry 691, 695 (2024).

                                            6
[L275] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 7 / 39>[L276] Whether the Rehabilitation Act or ADA Impose or Authorize an Integration Mandate

[L278] (citation omitted). In-patient treatment, he explained, can fit that rubric,
[L279] though not “always” or “by [its] nature.” Id. at 614. When, “without
[L280] adequate justification,” states expose patients with mental disabilities “to
[L281] more onerous treatment than a comparison group” in providing medical
[L282] services, this “irrational” distinction is discriminatory. Id. at 611. Hence,
[L283] it may amount to “discrimination on the basis of mental disability” if
[L284] “individuals suffering from medical problems of comparable seriousness”
[L285] receive treatment in “the most integrated setting appropriate for the treat-
[L286] ment of those problems,” but mentally disabled patients do not. Id. at 612.
[L287] Justice Kennedy further recognized that every state “must make hard
[L288] decisions on how much to allocate to treatment of diseases and disabili-
[L289] ties,” id., and that they must “not be forced to create a community-
[L290] treatment program where none exists,” id. at 613.
[L291]    Third, Justice Thomas, joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justice
[L292] Scalia, dissented, based primarily on the textual meaning of “discrimina-
[L293] tion.” As noted, Justice Thomas shared—in fact, supplied—Justice Ken-
[L294] nedy’s formulation of the ordinary meaning of discrimination as “differ-
[L295] ential treatment vis-à-vis members of a different group on the basis of a
[L296] statutorily described characteristic.” Id. at 616 (Thomas, J., dissenting).
[L297] But unlike Justice Kennedy, Justice Thomas concluded that a state’s
[L298] decision to treat some patients with mental disabilities in institutions—
[L299] regardless of whether it uses more integrated settings for other patients—
[L300] can never “amount to ‘discrimination’ in the traditional sense of the
[L301] word.” Id. Such treatment decisions, he maintained, show only that “some
[L302] members of a protected group [here, mentally disabled persons] are treat-
[L303] ed differently from other members of that same group.” Id. at 622–23.
[L304] And “dissimilar treatment” between disabled and nondisabled persons,
[L305] Justice Thomas observed, often “results merely from the fact that different
[L306] classes of persons receive different services—not from ‘discrimination’ as
[L307] traditionally defined.” Id. at 625. In Justice Thomas’s view, rather than
[L308] prohibiting differential treatment of “similarly situated persons,” the
[L309] majority read Title II to impose a specific “standard of care” for patients
[L310] with mental disabilities treated by the states. Id. at 623.

                                       B.

[L314]   Properly understood, Olmstead did not conclusively resolve your re-
[L315] maining questions, thus requiring any interested parties to “navigate . . .
                                        7
[L318] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 8 / 39>[L319]                            50 Op. O.L.C. __ (June 18, 2026)

[L321] the murky waters between” the constitutional, statutory, and regulatory
[L322] provisions at play on their own. Arc of Wash. State Inc. v. Braddock, 427
[L323] F.3d 615, 617 (9th Cir. 2005). When the Court splinters on the rationale
[L324] for its judgment, we are to look for the “position taken by those Members
[L325] who concurred in the judgment[] on the narrowest grounds.” Marks v.
[L326] United States, 430 U.S. 188, 193 (1977) (citation omitted). In this in-
[L327] stance, there were not five votes for the proposition that Title II imposes
[L328] an integration mandate on states—let alone that such a mandate would
[L329] pass constitutional muster.
[L330]    Five justices agreed that “unjustified institutional isolation of persons
[L331] with disabilities is a form of discrimination” prohibited under Title II.
[L332] Olmstead, 527 U.S. at 600. Olmstead offers remarkably little guidance,
[L333] however, about the circumstances under which in-patient—that is, institu-
[L334] tional—treatment is unjustified. Recall Justice Ginsburg’s view that
[L335] “States are required to provide community-based treatment” when three
[L336] factors are present, namely when: (1) an individual’s “treatment profes-
[L337] sionals determine that such placement is appropriate,” (2) that individual
[L338] “do[es] not oppose such treatment,” and (3) “the placement can be rea-
[L339] sonably accommodated, taking into account the resources available to the
[L340] State and the needs of others with mental disabilities.” Id. at 607 (plurality
[L341] opinion) (emphasis added). But that view appears only in sections of the
[L342] opinion that expressly are not the opinion of the Court. See id. at 587
[L343] (opinion of the Court limited to “Parts I, II, and III-A”).8 Thus, Olmstead
[L344] did not conclusively resolve which justifications a state may offer in
[L345] defense of its treatment choices—it held only that institutionalization
[L346] must be “[]justified.” Id. at 600 (majority opinion).
[L347]    The Court’s majority did make clear that it was not “determin[ing] the[]
[L348] validity” of the HHS and DOJ regulations, meaning it had no occasion to
[L349] decide whether “the regulatory formulations themselves [are] outside the

[L351]    8 The paragraph appearing after the dinkus—the “set of three asterisks . . . used to di-

[L353] vide sections of text,” Joe Fore, Ending a Section with Style, 71 Va. Law. 54, 54 (2023)
[L354] (emphasis omitted)—is not part of the majority opinion and indeed cites parts of the
[L355] plurality’s reasoning from Part III-B that the Court’s deciding votes expressly did not
[L356] join. Compare Olmstead, 527 U.S. at 607 (discussing whether institutional “placement
[L357] can be reasonably accommodated, taking into account the resources available to the
[L358] State”), with id. at 604 (plurality opinion) (describing “the reasonable-modifications
[L359] regulation” designed to “allow the State to show that, in the allocation of available
[L360] resources, immediate relief for the [disabled] would be inequitable”).

                                            8
[L364] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 9 / 39>[L365] Whether the Rehabilitation Act or ADA Impose or Authorize an Integration Mandate

[L367] congressional authorization.” Id. at 592. To be sure, the Court cited the
[L368] regulations as persuasive authority for its holding that isolation could,
[L369] under some circumstances, amount to discrimination even without prefer-
[L370] ential treatment for similarly situated persons who do not have the same
[L371] disabilities. See id. at 597–98. But accepting that proposition does not
[L372] require a state to move institutionalized patients to “the most integrated
[L373] setting appropriate to the[ir] needs.” 28 C.F.R. § 35.130(d). In other
[L374] words, stating that institutional isolation can be discriminatory does not
[L375] equate to saying that it is discriminatory under specific circumstances.
[L376]    One counterargument, which the Seventh Circuit has accepted, is that
[L377] the first two factors proposed by the plurality—professional determination
[L378] of fitness for community-based treatment and patient opposition to care in
[L379] an in-patient setting—should be deemed part of the Court’s holding
[L380] because they “appear in Section III.A of the Olmstead decision.” Steimel
[L381] v. Wernert, 823 F.3d 902, 914 (7th Cir. 2016). The majority opinion
[L382] certainly references “the reasonable assessments of [a state’s] profession-
[L383] als” and patient “desire” as relevant to the question of whether institution-
[L384] alization—that is, the provision of care in an in-patient setting, typically
[L385] over the medium or long term—is justified in a given case. Olmstead, 527
[L386] U.S. at 602. But not even the Olmstead plurality held that Title II makes
[L387] maximal integration obligatory based on these factors alone. Given the
[L388] dire consequences it has already spawned for so many, see supra note 7,
[L389] we decline to go further than Olmstead clearly required by its limited
[L390] majority rule. Cf. Richard M. Re, Beyond the Marks Rule, 132 Harv. L.
[L391] Rev. 1943 (2019) (discussing the difficulties in applying the Marks “nar-
[L392] rowest grounds” framework); Adam Steinman, Nonmajority Opinions and
[L393] Biconditional Rules, 128 Yale L.J.F. 1, 2–3 (2018) (same).
[L394]    With respect to professional assessment and patient consent, the
[L395] Olmstead majority opinion says only that these factors can justify so-
[L396] called institutionalization. Specifically, the Court said that “the State
[L397] generally may rely on the reasonable assessments of its own professionals
[L398] in determining whether an individual ‘meets the essential eligibility
[L399] requirements’ for habilitation in a community-based program.” 527 U.S.
[L400] at 602 (emphasis added). The Court further observed that there is no
[L401] “federal requirement that community-based treatment be imposed on
[L402] patients who do not desire it.” Id.

                                        9
[L406] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 10 / 39>[L407]                            50 Op. O.L.C. __ (June 18, 2026)

[L409]    But it is a logical fallacy to say that the Court necessarily held the in-
[L410] verse: that without these factors a public entity cannot justify treatment in
[L411] an institutional setting.9 Indeed, the majority explained that it offered
[L412] these factors to “emphasize that nothing in the ADA or its implementing
[L413] regulations condones termination of institutional settings for persons
[L414] unable to handle or benefit from community settings.” Id. at 601–02. Read
[L415] in this light, the opinion permits treatment in an institution based on
[L416] professional assessment and patient consent. It does not say that these
[L417] factors are the only acceptable justifications. Such statements that Title II
[L418] “require[s] placement of persons with mental disabilities in community
[L419] settings rather than in institutions” appear only in portions of the
[L420] Olmstead opinion written by the plurality. Id. at 587 (plurality opinion);
[L421] see also id. at 607.
[L422]    A second counterargument is that Olmstead took at least some justifica-
[L423] tions off the table when it rejected Georgia’s argument that the choice to
[L424] institutionalize a patient “due to insufficient space in the program, insuffi-
[L425] cient federal or state resources, or safety concerns” was not based on
[L426] disability but on other factors. Brief for Petitioners at 20, Olmstead, 527
[L427] U.S. 581 (No. 98-536). As noted above, the Court implicitly repudiated
[L428] that argument (without addressing the legitimacy of the cited rationales),
[L429] along with the argument about the need for a comparator to establish
[L430] “discrimination.” See Olmstead, 527 U.S. at 598. Importantly, the two
[L431] rejected arguments were distinct textual moves, one about the meaning of
[L432] “discrimination” and the other about the meaning of “by reason of.” Cf.
[L433] Univ. of Tex. Sw. Med. Ctr. v. Nassar, 570 U.S. 338, 350–52 (2013).
[L434] Although the Court rejected the view that program capacity, resource
[L435] constraints, and safety concerns automatically break the causal link be-
[L436] tween disability and discrimination, it did not decide whether—because
[L437] Georgia did not argue that—those considerations were sufficient justifica-
[L438] tions for in-patient treatment in an institution. Cf. Cooper Indus., Inc. v.

[L440]    9 See NLRB v. Noel Canning, 573 U.S. 513, 589 (2014) (Scalia, J., concurring in the

[L442] judgment) (discussing “the fallacy of the inverse (otherwise known as denying the
[L443] antecedent)” as “the incorrect assumption that if P implies Q, then not-P implies not-Q”);
[L444] see also, e.g., United States v. Holland, 117 F.4th 1352, 1359 (11th Cir. 2024) (same);
[L445] Memorandum for the Legal Advisor, National Security Council, from T. Elliot Gaiser,
[L446] Assistant Attorney General, Office of Legal Counsel, Re: Proposed War Department
[L447] Operation to Support Law Enforcement Efforts in Venezuela at 16 (Dec. 23, 2025).

[L451] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 11 / 39>[L452] Whether the Rehabilitation Act or ADA Impose or Authorize an Integration Mandate

[L454] Aviall Servs., Inc., 543 U.S. 157, 170 (2004). If they are, then such institu-
[L455] tional treatment is not discriminatory in the first place, meaning there is
[L456] no need to reach the second question of whether discrimination is “by
[L457] reason of” disability.
[L458]    Looking only to those aspects of the opinion that represent the law, we
[L459] conclude that Olmstead did not hold that Title II requires maximal inte-
[L460] gration for patients with mental disabilities receiving state treatment.
[L461] Rather, it held only that a state cannot institutionalize such patients with-
[L462] out justification. See 527 U.S. at 600 (majority opinion). What counts as
[L463] adequate justification remains an open question.

                                          C.

[L467]    We recognize that this view of Olmstead’s import is out of step with
[L468] the common understanding of that decision within the federal courts.
[L469] Olmstead is typically thought to have “reified” the integration mandate as
[L470] codified in HHS and DOJ regulations. United States v. Mississippi, 82
[L471] F.4th 387, 388 (5th Cir. 2023). Moreover, the vast majority of federal
[L472] courts of appeals treats as binding the plurality’s statements that Title II
[L473] “require[s]” deinstitutionalization when the three listed factors are met.
[L474] Olmstead, 527 U.S. at 607.10 There is consequently a risk that any final
[L475] agency action adopting our view will be subject to challenge in litigation
[L476] under the Administrative Procedure Act. See 5 U.S.C. § 706(2). Moreo-
[L477] ver, any state that chooses to treat a person with mental disabilities in an
[L478] institution based on our reasoning may still be subject to individual
[L479] “Olmstead claims” seeking a judicial order to release party patients. See
[L480] Barnes v. Gorman, 536 U.S. 181, 185 (2002).

[L486] Cir. 2025); Harrison ex rel. Harrison v. Young, 103 F.4th 1132, 1138–39 (5th Cir. 2024);
[L487] Waskul ex rel. Waskul v. Washtenaw Cnty. Cmty. Mental Health, 979 F.3d 426, 460 n.14
[L488] (6th Cir. 2020); United States v. Florida, 938 F.3d 1221, 1250 (11th Cir. 2019); Par-
[L489] ent/Pro. Advoc. League v. City of Springfield, 934 F.3d 13, 18–19 (1st Cir. 2019); Brown

[L497] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 12 / 39>[L498]                        50 Op. O.L.C. __ (June 18, 2026)

[L500]    But our legal system is built on the idea that “contested legal ques-
[L501] tions,” especially those concerning Executive Branch practices, should be
[L502] permitted “to percolate and potentially be resolved by the political
[L503] branches in the democratic process.” FDA v. All. for Hippocratic Med.,
[L504] 144 S. Ct. 1540, 1555 (2024). In that system, it is the duty of the Supreme
[L505] Court to assess the meaning and vitality of its opinions regarding the laws
[L506] that Congress has passed. Cf. Trump v. CASA, Inc., 145 S. Ct. 2540,
[L507] 2550–51 (2025); United States v. Mendoza, 464 U.S. 154, 160 (1984). At
[L508] the same time, it is the President’s duty to “take Care that [such] Laws be
[L509] faithfully executed.” U.S. Const. art. II, § 3. And it is our duty to provide
[L510] an independent assessment of what faithful execution means—even if it
[L511] requires disagreeing with a federal court so that the question can receive
[L512] adversarial testing. See Whether Eluding Inspection Under 8 U.S.C.
[L513] § 1325(a)(2) Is a Continuing Offense, 49 Op. O.L.C. __, at *17 (June 21,
[L514] 2025) (“Eluding Inspection”).
[L515]    In our good-faith and independent judgment, Olmstead does not con-
[L516] clusively hold that Title II (or section 504) mandates maximal integration
[L517] in state treatment of mentally disabled patients. It certainly does not
[L518] resolve the question of whether Congress may constitutionally impose an
[L519] integration mandate—a presumption which was “neither brought to the
[L520] attention of the court nor ruled upon” and thus is “not to be considered . . .
[L521] precedent[].” Webster v. Fall, 266 U.S. 507, 511 (1925).

                                     II.

[L525]    Having concluded that Olmstead does not resolve your questions, we
[L526] would normally turn next to your statutory question—whether Congress
[L527] imposed an integration mandate—under the canon of constitutional
[L528] avoidance. See Eluding Inspection at *10–11. Our analysis of your statu-
[L529] tory question, however, raised grave doubts regarding whether reading
[L530] section 504 and Title II to impose a universal integration mandate on
[L531] states would tread on fundamental principles of federalism and exceed the
[L532] scope of Congress’s powers under Section 5 of the Fourteenth Amend-
[L533] ment as well as the Interstate Commerce and Spending Clauses. Under
[L534] such circumstances, the avoidance canon imposes a “‘clarity tax’ on
[L535] Congress” in order to “advance values external to a statute.” Biden v.
[L536] Nebraska, 143 S. Ct. 2355, 2376–77 (2023) (Barrett, J., concurring)

                                     12
[L540] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 13 / 39>[L541] Whether the Rehabilitation Act or ADA Impose or Authorize an Integration Mandate

[L543] (quoting John F. Manning, Clear Statement Rules and the Constitution,
[L544] 110 Colum. L. Rev. 399, 403 (2010)). Because that clarity tax necessarily
[L545] informs our statutory analysis, we explain our constitutional concerns
[L546] before turning to the enacted text. 11

                                            A.

[L550]    We start with foundational principles of federalism that must always
[L551] guide our analysis when, as here, the burden of federal policy falls upon
[L552] states. The dual sovereignty of the federal and state governments reflects
[L553] “a fundamental structural decision incorporated into the Constitution.”
[L554] Murphy v. Nat’l Collegiate Athletic Ass’n, 584 U.S. 453, 470 (2018).
[L555] “The Constitution limited but did not abolish the sovereign powers of the
[L556] States, which retained ‘a residuary and inviolable sovereignty.’” Id. (cita-
[L557] tion omitted); accord The Federalist No. 39, at 256 (James Madison)
[L558] (Jacob E. Cooke ed., 1961). “[I]f a power is an attribute of state sover-
[L559] eignty reserved [to the states] by the Tenth Amendment, it is necessarily a
[L560] power the Constitution has not conferred on Congress.” New York v.
[L561] United States, 505 U.S. 144, 156 (1992). And the Supreme Court has
[L562] specifically warned not to overread the three powers that Congress in-
[L563] voked to pass section 504 and Title II, lest they “subver[t] . . . the gov-
[L564] ernmental powers reserved to the individual states.” United States v.
[L565] Butler, 297 U.S. 1, 75 (1936) (Spending Clause); City of Boerne v. Flores,
[L566] 521 U.S. 507, 534–35 (1997) (Fourteenth Amendment); United States v.
[L567] Lopez, 514 U.S. 549, 564–68 (1995) (Commerce Clause); see also Gib-
[L568] bons v. Ogden, 22 U.S. (9 Wheat.) 1, 204–06 (1824) (same).


[L571]    11 For the avoidance of doubt, nothing in this memorandum should be interpreted to

[L573] question the facial constitutionality of either section 504 or Title II, which extend far
[L574] beyond the integration mandate as it has been applied to the type of mental disabilities
[L575] directly at issue in Olmstead. Congress certainly has a number of tools in its kit by which
[L576] it can address discrimination in its myriad forms, including discrimination on the basis of
[L577] disability (whether mental, physical, or both). We question only whether various constitu-
[L578] tional principles permit Congress, in passing broadly worded statutes such as section 504
[L579] or Title II, to impose a mandate on states that has cut through those states’ mental-health
[L580] programs like a chainsaw. To the extent Congress can mandate integration of the states’
[L581] mentally disabled patients, we believe the Constitution requires more precise implementa-
[L582] tion. The constitutionality of any other application of either statute is beyond the scope of
[L583] this opinion.

                                            13
[L587] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 14 / 39>[L588]                        50 Op. O.L.C. __ (June 18, 2026)

[L590]    In interpreting the reach of Congress’s enumerated powers, then, we
[L591] must be careful to remember that Congress typically cannot compel the
[L592] states “to govern according to [its] instructions.” New York, 505 U.S. at
[L593] 162. Nor may it imperil the states’ sovereign powers over “all the objects,
[L594] which, in the ordinary course of affairs, concern the lives, liberties, and
[L595] properties of the people; and the internal order, improvement, and pros-
[L596] perity of the State.” The Federalist No. 45, at 313 (James Madison). True,
[L597] “Congress may legislate in areas traditionally regulated by the States,” but
[L598] that “is a power that we must assume Congress does not exercise lightly.”
[L599] Gregory v. Ashcroft, 501 U.S. 452, 460 (1991). Thus, “if Congress intends
[L600] to alter the ‘usual constitutional balance between the States and the Feder-
[L601] al Government,’ it must make its intention to do so ‘unmistakably clear in
[L602] the language of the statute.’” Will v. Mich. Dep’t of State Police, 491 U.S.
[L603] 58, 65 (1989) (quoting Atascadero State Hosp. v. Scanlon, 473 U.S. 234,
[L604] 242 (1985)).
[L605]    A mandate that states undertake not only the duty to provide medical
[L606] care for those with mental disabilities but the obligation to do so in the
[L607] setting preferred by the federal government would trigger this clear-
[L608] statement rule because such a mandate would “upset the usual constitu-
[L609] tional balance of federal and state powers.” Gregory, 501 U.S. at 460.
[L610] “[T]he regulation of health and safety matters is primarily, and historical-
[L611] ly, a matter of local concern.” Hillsborough County v. Automated Med.
[L612] Labs., Inc., 471 U.S. 707, 719 (1985). Consequently, there are clear
[L613] “federalism costs inherent in [subjecting] state decisions regarding the
[L614] administration of treatment programs and the allocation of resources to”
[L615] federal control. Olmstead, 527 U.S. at 610 (Kennedy, J., concurring in the
[L616] judgment); see also id. at 624–25 (Thomas, J., dissenting). Thus, we must
[L617] tread carefully in interpreting both the positive reach of Congress’s pow-
[L618] ers to legislate and how it exercised those powers, lest we trample the
[L619] principle of federalism inherent in our constitutional structure.

                                     B.

[L623]   With those principles in mind, we turn first to the integration mandate
[L624] putatively imposed by Title II, the statute directly at issue in Olmstead.
[L625] Congress passed the ADA pursuant to both its “power to enforce the
[L626] fourteenth amendment and to regulate commerce.” 42 U.S.C.
                                     14
[L629] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 15 / 39>[L630] Whether the Rehabilitation Act or ADA Impose or Authorize an Integration Mandate

[L632] § 12101(b)(4).12 On their face, neither constitutional provision clearly
[L633] authorizes Congress to dictate where state and local programs must pro-
[L634] vide services to individuals with mental disabilities.

                                           1.

[L638]    Having “expand[ed] federal power at the expense of state autonomy,”
[L639] Seminole Tribe of Fla. v. Florida, 517 U.S. 44, 59 (1996), the Fourteenth
[L640] Amendment provides Congress considerable leeway to ensure that “all
[L641] persons similarly situated should be treated alike,” City of Cleburne v.
[L642] Cleburne Living Ctr., Inc., 473 U.S. 432, 439 (1985). For Congress to
[L643] invoke its authority for enforcing equal protection, however, “there must
[L644] be a pattern of discrimination by the States which violates the Fourteenth
[L645] Amendment, and the remedy imposed by Congress must be congruent and
[L646] proportional to the targeted violation.” Bd. of Trs. of the Univ. of Ala. v.
[L647] Garrett, 531 U.S. 356, 374 (2001); cf. Louisiana v. Callais, 146 S. Ct.
[L648] 1131, 1155 (2026) (explaining that Congress may only “enforce a right
[L649] that the Amendment secures”). In other words, Congress’s power under
[L650] Section 5 is purely “remedial and preventive,” aimed solely at addressing
[L651] state conduct that violates the Fourteenth Amendment. Boerne, 521 U.S.
[L652] at 524.
[L653]    Even assuming that in-patient treatment of individuals with mental dis-
[L654] abilities can be considered discrimination, it is not the kind of discrimina-
[L655] tion forbidden by the Fourteenth Amendment unless it is entirely unsup-
[L656] ported by any rational justification. As the Supreme Court has reiterated
[L657] time and again, the Equal Protection Clause “was surely not intended to
[L658] make every discrimination between groups of people” unconstitutional.
[L659] Oregon v. Mitchell, 400 U.S. 112, 127 (1970); see also, e.g., San Antonio
[L660] Indep. Sch. Dist. v. Rodriguez, 411 U.S. 1, 24 (1973). “[W]here individu-
[L661] als in the group affected by a law have distinguishing characteristics
[L662] relevant to interests the State has the authority to implement,” there is
[L663] often a legitimate basis for treating those individuals differently from
[L664] others. Cleburne Living Ctr., 473 U.S. at 441. Such is the case with men-

[L666]    12 In passing Title II, Congress purported to “invoke the sweep of congressional au-

[L668] thority.” 42 U.S.C. § 12101(b)(4). We can think of no alternative source of congressional
[L669] authority that would justify the integration mandate where the Constitution’s most
[L670] capacious grants of legislative power fail to do so.

                                           15
[L674] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 16 / 39>[L675]                             50 Op. O.L.C. __ (June 18, 2026)

[L677] tally disabled persons. Because they have different treatment needs than
[L678] their nondisabled peers, the Supreme Court has squarely held that “mental
[L679] [disability] is a characteristic that the government may legitimately take
[L680] into account in a wide range of decisions.” Id. at 446. The Court has also
[L681] held that “States are not required by the Fourteenth Amendment to make
[L682] special accommodations for the disabled, so long as their actions toward
[L683] such individuals are rational.” Garrett, 531 U.S. at 367. Thus, “classifica-
[L684] tions based on disability” violate equal protection only “if they lack a
[L685] rational relationship to a legitimate governmental purpose.” Tennessee v.
[L686] Lane, 541 U.S. 509, 522 (2004).
[L687]    Taking as a given Olmstead’s holding that long-term in-patient care—
[L688] what Olmstead called “institutionalization”—may be irrational in some
[L689] instances, Congress has the authority to remedy such arbitrary discrimina-
[L690] tion against people with disabilities. Id. But it would take a strong legisla-
[L691] tive record to demonstrate that a universal mandate of maximal integra-
[L692] tion for mentally disabled persons is “congruent and proportional” to
[L693] existing state violations. Garrett, 531 U.S. at 374.
[L694]    Olmstead itself suggests why a universal integration mandate is unlike-
[L695] ly to pass scrutiny. As every member of the Olmstead Court recognized,
[L696] treating mentally disabled people in institutions, even when community-
[L697] based treatment is a viable option, is not irrational per se.13 States may
[L698] have many legitimate reasons for doing so, including resource constraints,
[L699] capacity limitations in community-based facilities, and safety concerns for
[L700] both the patient and the community. See, e.g., Addington v. Texas, 441
[L701] U.S. 418, 426 (1979); Frederick L. v. Dep’t of Pub. Welfare of Pa., 364
[L702] F.3d 487, 497–98 (3d Cir. 2004); Jackson ex rel. Jackson v. Fort Stanton
[L703] Hosp. & Training Sch., 964 F.2d 980, 992 (10th Cir. 1992).
[L704]    Because institutional treatment “is not invidious nor palpably arbi-
[L705] trary,” it does not, as a general matter, violate the Fourteenth Amendment.

[L707]    13 Olmstead, 527 U.S. at 603 (majority opinion) (allowing states to rely on the deter-

[L709] minations of their own treatment professionals regarding what treatment setting is appro-
[L710] priate); id. at 607 (Stevens, J., concurring in part and concurring in the judgment) (affirm-
[L711] ing the decision that the district court should consider the state’s “fundamental-alteration
[L712] defense”); id. at 614 (Kennedy, J., concurring in the judgment) (noting that institutionali-
[L713] zation is not “always discriminatory”); id. at 625 (Thomas, J., dissenting) (observing that
[L714] the “dissimilar treatment” observed in Olmstead “result[ed] merely from the fact that
[L715] different classes of persons receive different services”).

[L719] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 17 / 39>[L720] Whether the Rehabilitation Act or ADA Impose or Authorize an Integration Mandate

[L722] Allied Stores of Ohio, Inc. v. Bowers, 358 U.S. 522, 530 (1959). As a
[L723] result, a universal mandate to maximally integrate mentally disabled state
[L724] patients would not be “remedial” because the conduct it targets—
[L725] institutional treatment—is generally not violative of the Fourteenth
[L726] Amendment. Boerne, 521 U.S. at 519 (citation omitted). 14
[L727]    No sufficient legislative record exists to justify an integration mandate
[L728] on states as a remedial measure against irrational discrimination.
[L729] Olmstead relied in large part on two congressional findings to conclude
[L730] that Title II prohibits isolating disabled people in some instances, see 527
[L731] U.S. at 599–600, but neither finding is even specific to states or to the so-
[L732] called institutionalization of the mentally disabled, see 42 U.S.C.
[L733] § 12101(a)(2), (5). They certainly do not purport to find a pattern of states
[L734] institutionalizing mentally disabled patients for entirely arbitrary rea-
[L735] sons—which pattern might justify legislation under Section 5. Moreover,
[L736] like any other antidiscrimination statute that depends on the Reconstruc-
[L737] tion Amendments for constitutional legitimacy, the “statute’s ‘current
[L738] burdens’ must be justified by ‘current needs’”—not “decades-old data and
[L739] eradicated practices.” Shelby County v. Holder, 570 U.S. 529, 550–51
[L740] (2013) (citation omitted). As the integration mandate imposed under
[L741] Title II is now more than thirty-five years old, its vague findings about the
[L742] social ills associated with discrimination against those with disabilities
[L743] would likely be insufficient to justify the significant burden that the

                                             2.

[L774]    The Commerce Clause also likely provides too thin a reed to support a
[L775] generally applicable integration mandate. The scope of Congress’s power
[L776] to regulate interstate commerce is unquestionably “broad.” NFIB v. Sebe-
[L777] lius, 567 U.S. 519, 549 (2012) (opinion of Roberts, C.J.); accord Katzen-
[L778] bach v. McClung, 379 U.S. 294, 305 (1964). But like any other power in
[L779] Article I, it “has limits,” Maryland v. Wirtz, 392 U.S. 183, 196 (1968),
[L780] particularly in core areas of state responsibility such as “provid[ing] for
[L781] the health of its citizens,” Gibbons, 22 U.S. (9 Wheat.) at 205. It cannot
[L782] reach “noneconomic . . . conduct based solely on that conduct’s aggregate
[L783] effect on interstate commerce.” Morrison, 529 U.S. at 617. And it cannot
[L784] “be pushed to such an extreme as to destroy the distinction . . . between
[L785] commerce ‘among the several States’ and the internal concerns of a
[L786] State.” NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel Corp., 301 U.S. 1, 30 (1937).
[L787]    A mandate of where states provide healthcare to patients with mental
[L788] disabilities within their own borders goes beyond any approved exercise
[L789] of Congress’s power over interstate commerce of which we are aware. Of
[L790] course, some aspects of state healthcare may affect interstate commerce
[L791] such that they are subject to federal regulation. Cf. Gonzalez v. Raich, 545
[L792] U.S. 1, 18–19 (2005). For example, the decision whether to provide such
[L793] care is in some sense “an economic activity that might, through repetition
[L794] elsewhere, substantially affect . . . interstate commerce.” Lopez, 514 U.S.
[L795] at 567. But that is not what is at issue in the context of the integration
[L796] mandate. Instead, the only question implicated here is the “setting” of
[L797] treatment. E.g., Olmstead, 527 U.S. at 602 (citing 28 C.F.R. § 35.130(d)).
[L798] A choice by the state, among treatment facilities within the state, for
