[L803] ity would be immune from these limits—particularly given that the limits apply even
[L804] when Congress is legislating to eliminate racial discrimination, which serves “the central
[L805] purpose of the Fourteenth Amendment.” McLaughlin v. Florida, 379 U.S. 184, 192
[L806] (1964); cf. United States v. Skrmetti, 145 S. Ct. 1816, 1862 (2025) (Alito, J., concurring in
[L807] part and concurring in the judgment) (discussing Shelby County in the context of alleged
[L808] gender-identity discrimination).

[L815] patients of the state falls on the “local” side of the line between that which
[L816] is national and that which is local, a line which our federalism demands
[L817] be maintained. Lopez, 514 U.S. at 567–68; see also Morrison, 529 U.S. at
[L818] 617–18. At most, any marginal effect that a state’s choice to treat mental-
[L819] ly ill patients in institutional settings may have on the national economy is
[L820] “attenuated,” making it less likely that Title II would survive constitution-
[L821] al scrutiny under the Commerce Clause if the statute were read to include
[L822] an integration mandate. Morrison, 529 U.S. at 612. 16
[L823]    Our concerns are not assuaged by the fact that Congress has, with the
[L824] Supreme Court’s blessing, invoked the Commerce Clause to regulate
[L825] discrimination, particularly by private parties. See Heart of Atlanta Motel,
[L826] Inc. v. United States, 379 U.S. 241, 261–62 (1964); McClung, 379 U.S. at
[L827] 304–05. The Court has made clear that discrimination targeted under the
[L828] Clause may occur purely within a single state, but it must still involve
[L829] “persons or things in interstate commerce” or “activities that substantially
[L830] affect interstate commerce.” Lopez, 514 U.S. at 558–59. Thus, antidis-
[L831] crimination laws previously upheld as legitimate exercises of the com-
[L832] merce power either prohibited “obstructions . . . in interstate commerce,”
[L833] Heart of Atlanta Motel, 379 U.S. at 261, or regulated “establishments
[L834] having a close tie to interstate commerce,” McClung, 379 U.S. at 304.
[L835] Mentally disabled people are people, not objects in interstate commerce.
[L836] Cf. U.S. Const. amend. XIII (forbidding commerce in human beings). Nor
[L837] has Congress made findings to the effect that interstate commerce is
[L838] affected by whether a state treats disabled patients within its care in an
[L839] institution, a group home, or their own homes. See 42 U.S.C.
[L840] § 12101(a).17 Although not dispositive, the absence of legislative findings

                                            C.

[L869]    Turning next to section 504, although admittedly a closer question, the
[L870] integration mandate could raise serious constitutional concerns if based on
[L871] Congress’s spending power. By conditioning the receipt of “Federal
[L872] financial assistance” on a lack of discrimination against disabled people,
[L873] 29 U.S.C. § 794(a), Congress invoked its constitutional authority to “fix
[L874] the terms on which it shall disburse federal money,” Cummings v. Premier
[L875] Rehab Keller, PLLC, 142 S. Ct. 1562, 1569 (2022) (citation omitted).
[L876] Like any other power granted to the federal government, however, the
[L877] spending power has limits. E.g., Butler, 297 U.S. at 75; supra Part II.A.
[L878] Because there is no clear hook for the mandate in section 504’s text, it
[L879] likely transgresses those limits.
[L880]    Longstanding practice and judicial precedent have recognized that
[L881] when Congress spends money to “provide for . . . the general Welfare of
[L882] the United States,” U.S. Const. art. I, § 8, cl. 1, it may “place conditions
[L883] on the grant of federal funds,” Barnes, 536 U.S. at 185–86. By so doing,
[L884] Congress can “induce the States [and private actors] to adopt policies that
[L885] the Federal Government itself could not impose.” Sebelius, 567 U.S. at
[L886] 537. But “[t]he legitimacy of Congress’ power to legislate under the
[L887] spending power . . . rests on whether the State [or private actor] voluntari-
[L888] ly and knowingly accepts the terms” of the funding conditions. Pennhurst
[L889] State Sch. & Hosp. v. Halderman, 451 U.S. 1, 17 (1981).
[L890]    In the light of these principles, Congress surely could condition some
[L891] amount of federal funds on maximal integration for disabled persons. See


[L894] merce arising out of the interstate movement of patients”). Even if the treatment setting of
[L895] a single individual does not affect interstate commerce, the aggregate effect of an insur-
[L896] ance company’s activities may do so within the meaning of current precedent. See United
[L897] States v. S.-E. Underwriters Ass’n, 322 U.S. 533, 553 (1944) (“No commercial enterprise
[L898] of any kind which conducts its activities across state lines has been held to be wholly
[L899] beyond the regulatory power of Congress under the Commerce Clause. We cannot make
[L900] an exception of the business of insurance.”). Similarly, even if some state patients cross
[L901] state lines, that fact would not empower Congress to regulate any state’s relationship with
[L902] all its patients, including those who are treated entirely within the state’s borders.

                                            20
[L906] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 21 / 39>[L907] Whether the Rehabilitation Act or ADA Impose or Authorize an Integration Mandate

[L909] id. But, again, there are limits. For example, Congress likely could not
[L910] “threat[en] to terminate other significant independent grants” unless a
[L911] state provides maximally integrated care for disabled persons, as such a
[L912] law would likely cross the line into “indirectly coerc[ing] a State to adopt
[L913] a federal regulatory system as its own.” Sebelius, 567 U.S. at 578, 580
[L914] (opinion of Roberts, C.J.). It also could not condition the receipt of high-
[L915] way funding on the provision of care to mentally disabled patients in a
[L916] community-based setting because such a condition would be “unrelated
[L917] ‘to the federal interest in particular national projects or programs.’” South
[L918] Dakota v. Dole, 483 U.S. 203, 207–08 (1987) (quoting Massachusetts v.
[L919] United States, 435 U.S. 444, 461 (1978) (plurality opinion)). Most perti-
[L920] nent here, “if Congress intends to impose a condition on the grant of
[L921] federal moneys, it must do so unambiguously.” Pennhurst, 451 U.S. at 17;
[L922] cf. Osseo Area Schs., 145 S. Ct. at 1660 (Thomas, J., concurring) (ques-
[L923] tioning whether section 504 bans unintentional discrimination as a condi-
[L924] tion of federal funding, since “nothing in the [statutory] text conveys” that
[L925] was “Congress’s intent”).
[L926]    By invoking deference to a federal agency, see 527 U.S. at 597–98 (cit-
[L927] ing, inter alia, Skidmore v. Swift & Co., 323 U.S. 134, 139–40 (1944)),
[L928] even the Olmstead majority seems to have acknowledged that section 504
[L929] and Title II are (at best) ambiguous as to whether they impose an integra-
[L930] tion mandate, see, e.g., Riegel v. Medtronic, Inc., 552 U.S. 312, 326
[L931] (2008) (noting that Skidmore deference would apply only if “we had
[L932] found the statute ambiguous”). As a result, even if section 504 theoretical-
[L933] ly could be read to impose such a mandate on the receipt of federal
[L934] funding, it certainly did not “do so unambiguously.” Pennhurst, 451 U.S.
[L935] at 17.
[L936]    True, “Congress need not specifically identify and proscribe each con-
[L937] dition in the legislation.” Davis ex rel. LaShonda D. v. Monroe Cnty. Bd.
[L938] of Educ., 526 U.S. 629, 650 (1999) (cleaned up). But the statute must still
[L939] “proscribe[]” the relevant conduct “with sufficient clarity.” Id. Said dif-
[L940] ferently, though Congress can prohibit many unspecified activities by
[L941] using broad language in its funding conditions, such conditions validly
[L942] extend only to activities that clearly fall within the meaning of the lan-
[L943] guage used. Cf. Franklin v. Gwinnett Cnty. Pub. Schs., 503 U.S. 60, 75
[L944] (1992) (finding no Spending Clause defect because sexual harassment was
[L945] “[u]nquestionably” within the meaning of “discrimination” under the

                                       21
[L949] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 22 / 39>[L950]                            50 Op. O.L.C. __ (June 18, 2026)

[L952] relevant statute). Because maximal integration is not clearly encompassed
[L953] within the antidiscrimination provision of section 504, it cannot be a
[L954] condition of federal funding under Congress’s spending power. And as it
[L955] is the text of the statute that must clearly authorize a given condition,
[L956] legislative history cannot be used to save an ambiguous funding condi-
[L957] tion. Contra Frederick L. v. Dep’t of Pub. Welfare, 157 F. Supp. 2d 509,
[L958] 536 (E.D. Pa. 2001).
[L959]    Nor could we get out of the constitutional thicket by relying on federal
[L960] regulations given the language of section 504 (or Title II for that matter).
[L961] “[T]he ability to place conditions on federal grants ultimately comes from
[L962] the Spending Clause, which empowers Congress, not the Executive, to
[L963] spend for the general welfare.” Tex. Educ. Agency v. U.S. Dep’t of Educ.,
[L964] 992 F.3d 350, 362 (5th Cir. 2021); accord West Virginia v. U.S. Dep’t of
[L965] the Treasury, 59 F.4th 1124, 1147 (11th Cir. 2023). Because “[l]egislative
[L966] power . . . belongs to the legislative branch, and to no other,” FCC v.
[L967] Consumers’ Rsch., 145 S. Ct. 2482, 2496 (2025), it could merely raise a
[L968] different constitutional problem if HHS or DOJ created conditions that
[L969] Congress chose not to impose (or, at least, clearly allow the agency to
[L970] impose), see infra Part III.B; cf. Whitman v. Am. Trucking Assns., Inc.,
[L971] 531 U.S. 457, 472 (2001). As DOJ has explained in other fora, in matters
[L972] involving different statutes, there may be circumstances under which
[L973] Congress has delegated the power to impose additional conditions on
[L974] spending.18 But such gap-filling regulations are valid as conditions on
[L975] funding only to the extent they are indeed authorized by statute. See
[L976] Decker v. Nw. Env’t Def. Ctr., 568 U.S. 597, 609 (2013). As we will
[L977] explain below, the regulations imposing the integration mandate exceed
[L978] the regulatory authority conferred by section 504 and Title II. See infra
[L979] Part III.B.3.

                                          III.

[L983]    Fortunately, however, we need not resolve the many thorny constitu-
[L984] tional questions left open by Olmstead, due to our conclusion regarding
[L985] your statutory question—namely, that current HHS and DOJ regulations

[L987]    18 See, e.g., Motion for Stay Pending Appeal and Administrative Stay at 17, California

[L989] v. HHS, No. 25-2165 (1st Cir. Dec. 8, 2025); Reply Brief for Appellants at 10, City &
[L990] County of San Francisco v. Barr, 965 F.3d 753 (9th Cir. 2020) (No. 18-17308), Dkt. 60.

                                          22
[L994] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 23 / 39>[L995] Whether the Rehabilitation Act or ADA Impose or Authorize an Integration Mandate

[L997] incorrectly interpret section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act and Title II of
[L998] the ADA to impose an integration mandate on federal funding recipients
[L999] and states.
[L1000]    The next part of our analysis proceeds in two parts. First, we ask
[L1001] whether the best interpretation of the statutes requires maximal integra-
[L1002] tion. It does not. These statutes forbid “discrimination” based on disability
[L1003] in the context of government services and programs. 29 U.S.C. § 794(a);
[L1004] 42 U.S.C. § 12132. Consistent with Olmstead’s fundamental holding, the
[L1005] choice to treat a disabled patient in an institution can be unjustified and
[L1006] hence discriminatory, but only when there are no legitimate, nondiscrimi-
[L1007] natory factors that weigh in favor of it. Second, we evaluate whether the
[L1008] statutes authorize regulatory imposition of the integration mandate.
[L1009] Again, the answer is no. “When the constitutional violation is unequal
[L1010] treatment,” a state or “a court theoretically can cure that unequal treat-
[L1011] ment either by extending the benefits or burdens to the exempted class, or
[L1012] by nullifying the benefits or burdens for all.” Barr v. Am. Ass’n of Pol.
[L1013] Consultants, Inc., 140 S. Ct. 2335, 2354 (2020). By requiring states to
[L1014] extend community-based services to mentally disabled individuals, even
[L1015] when in-patient treatment is not discriminatory, the HHS and DOJ regula-
[L1016] tions provide such individuals a right to demand certain treatment services
[L1017] from states—a right that is not granted by either section 504 or Title II.
[L1018] Hence, the regulations are unlawful.

                                       A.

[L1022]    “The task of resolving the dispute over the meaning of [a statutory text]
[L1023] begins where all such inquiries must begin: with the language of the
[L1024] statute itself.” Nebraska v. Parker, 577 U.S. 481, 488 (2016) (alteration in
[L1025] original) (citation omitted). Absent “specialized definitions,” statutory
[L1026] terms are best understood according to their “ordinary meaning at the time
[L1027] Congress adopted them.” Niz-Chavez v. Garland, 141 S. Ct. 1474, 1480–
[L1028] 81 (2021). Such terms should also be read “in light of [a statute’s] con-
[L1029] text, structure, and related statutory provisions.” Exxon Mobil Corp. v.
[L1030] Allapattah Servs., Inc., 545 U.S. 546, 558 (2005). Under these fundamen-
[L1031] tal rules of statutory interpretation, we conclude that neither section 504
[L1032] nor Title II obliges regulated entities to provide services to individuals
[L1033] with disabilities in the most integrated setting possible. Instead, these

                                       23
[L1037] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 24 / 39>[L1038]                        50 Op. O.L.C. __ (June 18, 2026)

[L1040] statutes prohibit only arbitrary distinctions between individuals with
[L1041] similar medical needs.

                                     1.

[L1045]    By their text, both section 504 and Title II prohibit “discrimination”
[L1046] “by reason of . . . disability.” 29 U.S.C. § 794(a); 42 U.S.C. § 12132.
[L1047] Because neither provision supplies a specialized definition for “discrimi-
[L1048] nation,” we look to the term’s ordinary meaning at the time the relevant
[L1049] statutes were passed. Niz-Chavez, 141 S. Ct. at 1480; see also Sebelius v.
[L1050] Cloer, 569 U.S. 369, 376 (2013).
[L1051]    In 1973, when the Rehabilitation Act was passed, “discrimination” was
[L1052] commonly understood to mean “making a distinction in favor of or
[L1053] against[] a person or thing based on the group, class, or category to which
[L1054] that person or thing belongs rather than on individual merit.” The Random
[L1055] House Dictionary of the English Language 411 (1st ed. 1967) (“Random
[L1056] House”); see also Webster’s Third New International Dictionary 648
[L1057] (1966 ed.) (“Webster’s Third New International”) (“the act, practice, or an
[L1058] instance of discriminating categorically rather than individually”). These
[L1059] definitions remained constant through 1990, when Title II was enacted.
[L1060] See The Random House Dictionary of the English Language 564 (2d ed.
[L1061] 1987); Webster’s Third New International Dictionary 648 (1986 ed.). The
[L1062] “ordinary meaning” of discrimination at the relevant time thus was under-
[L1063] stood to be “treat[ing] groups that are similarly situated differently with-
[L1064] out sufficient justification.” Ala. Dep’t of Revenue v. CSX Transp., Inc.,
[L1065] 575 U.S. 21, 26 (2015) (cleaned up).
[L1066]    Judicial analysis of the term “discrimination” has consistently agreed
[L1067] with this understanding of the word. Interpreting Title VII of the Civil
[L1068] Rights Act of 1964—“the paradigmatic antidiscrimination law,”
[L1069] Olmstead, 527 U.S. at 616 (Thomas, J., dissenting)—the Supreme Court
[L1070] has explained that the statute was designed to prevent employers from
[L1071] “favor[ing] an identifiable group . . . over other employees.” Griggs v.
[L1072] Duke Power Co., 401 U.S. 424, 429–30 (1971) (emphasis added). The
[L1073] Court has applied the same understanding of discrimination when inter-
[L1074] preting section 504 itself. For instance, it has held that section 504 re-
[L1075] quires no more than “the evenhanded treatment of qualified handicapped
[L1076] persons” relative to nondisabled people. Se. Cmty. Coll. v. Davis, 442

                                     24
[L1080] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 25 / 39>[L1081] Whether the Rehabilitation Act or ADA Impose or Authorize an Integration Mandate

[L1083] U.S. 397, 410 (1979); accord Traynor v. Turnage, 485 U.S. 535, 548
[L1084] (1988). The same logic extends to Title II of the ADA, 42 U.S.C.
[L1085] § 12134(b), which Congress drafted to parallel section 504 and “generally
[L1086] [is] interpreted in pari materia,” Frame v. City of Arlington, 657 F.3d
[L1087] 215, 223 (5th Cir. 2011).
[L1088]    That traditional understanding does not, by its terms, denote an integra-
[L1089] tion mandate. Instead, it recognizes that differentiation amounts to
[L1090] “discrimination” only if the result is to “treat[] . . . similarly situated”
[L1091] people “differently” from disabled people—whether that latter category
[L1092] includes all people with disabilities or only those with a specific kind of
[L1093] disability—“without sufficient justification.” CSX Transp, 575 U.S. at 26
[L1094] (cleaned up). What matters is whether “individuals suffering from medical
[L1095] problems of comparable seriousness” yet without the relevant disability
[L1096] receive more favorable treatment than those with the disability. Olmstead,
[L1097] 527 U.S. at 612 (Kennedy, J., concurring in the judgment). The mere fact
[L1098] that one patient with disabilities is treated in an in-patient setting while
[L1099] another sharing the same disability is treated in a group home or at his
[L1100] own home “cannot prove ‘discrimination.’” Olmstead, 527 U.S. at 618
[L1101] (Thomas, J., dissenting).
[L1102]    This understanding of section 504 and Title II is also consistent with
[L1103] the larger statutory context of each, which demonstrates both that Con-
[L1104] gress knows how to mandate integration when it so chooses and that it did
[L1105] not so choose in enacting either of the relevant antidiscrimination provi-
[L1106] sions. This can be seen most plainly by looking to Title III of the ADA,
[L1107] which explicitly provides that public “accommodations shall be afforded
[L1108] to an individual with a disability in the most integrated setting appropriate
[L1109] to the needs of the individual.” 42 U.S.C. § 12182(b)(1)(B)).19 We pre-
[L1110] sume the omission from Title II of a similar integration guarantee was
[L1111] “intentional[].” City & County of San Francisco v. EPA, 145 S. Ct. 704,
[L1112] 713–14 (2025) (citation omitted). And because the ADA was the direct
[L1113] descendant of the Rehabilitation Act, the fact that Congress felt the need
[L1114] to expressly target segregation in Title III suggests that it did not under-


[L1117]   19 Further buttressing this conclusion, Titles I and III, but not Title II, list “segre-

[L1119] gat[ion]” as an impermissible form of discrimination. 42 U.S.C. §§ 12112(b)(1),
[L1120] 12182(b)(2)(A)(iii).

                                          25
[L1124] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 26 / 39>[L1125]                             50 Op. O.L.C. __ (June 18, 2026)

[L1127] stand its own language in section 504—which it copied into Title II—as
[L1128] proscribing such conduct. 20
[L1129]    Our understanding is also consistent with Title II’s historical context.
[L1130] In passing Title II, Congress acknowledged a long and sad history of
[L1131] unnecessary isolation and segregation of disabled individuals. 42 U.S.C.
[L1132] § 12101(a)(2), (5); see also U.S. Comm’n on Civ. Rts., Accommodating
[L1133] the Spectrum of Individual Abilities 40–41 (1983). But, as Justice Kenne-
[L1134] dy explained, “[t]hese findings do not show that segregation and institu-
[L1135] tionalization are always discriminatory or that segregation or institutional-
[L1136] ization are, by their nature, forms of prohibited discrimination.”
[L1137] Olmstead, 527 U.S. at 614 (Kennedy, J., concurring in the judgment)
[L1138] (emphases added). Rather, they “underscore Congress’ concern that,” as
[L1139] of 1990, “discrimination ha[d] been a frequent and pervasive problem in
[L1140] institutional settings and policies and its concern that segregating disabled
[L1141] persons from others can be discriminatory.” Id. Thus, we now turn to the
[L1142] key question left open by Olmstead: When does institutionalization treat
[L1143] similarly situated patients differently in a manner that is unjustified?

                                             2.

[L1147]    To start rooting out potential discrimination on the grounds of disabil-
[L1148] ity, one must first identify similarly situated patients. All too often, those
[L1149] seeking to eliminate past discrimination can create “classifications [that]
[L1150] rest on incoherent stereotypes” and “sweep[] into one pile” individuals
[L1151] who have little in common. Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. Presi-
[L1152] dent & Fellows of Harvard Coll., 143 S. Ct. 2141, 2210 (2023) (Gorsuch,
[L1153] J. concurring). This risk is particularly acute when it comes to mental
[L1154] illness and disability, both of which can come in innumerable shades of
[L1155] grey. See generally Am. Psychiatric Ass’n, DSM-5-TR, Diagnostic and
[L1156] Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (rev. 5th ed. 2022) (spanning

[L1158]    20 To be sure, a committee report suggests that some members of Congress (or their

[L1160] staffers) wanted “the forms of discrimination prohibited by [Title II to] be identical to
[L1161] those set out in the applicable provisions of [T]itles I and III.” H.R. Rep. No. 101-485,
[L1162] pt. 2, at 84 (1990). But “[w]hat Congress ultimately agrees on is the text that it enacts, not
[L1163] the preferences expressed by certain legislators.” NLRB v. SW Gen., Inc., 580 U.S. 288,
[L1164] 306 (2017). By contrast, enacted findings are part of the law that Congress passed and
[L1165] should be considered to the extent that they “inform application” of the operative text.
[L1166] Olmstead, 527 U.S. at 614 (Kennedy, J., concurring in the judgment).

[L1170] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 27 / 39>[L1171] Whether the Rehabilitation Act or ADA Impose or Authorize an Integration Mandate

[L1173] more than 1,100 pages). Not all community-based settings are appropriate
[L1174] for everyone who falls under the umbrella of mental disability. Often-
[L1175] times, an individual’s unique medical needs themselves justify institution-
[L1176] alization. Cf. Alexander v. Choate, 469 U.S. 287, 303 (1985). And it has
[L1177] been well understood since before Olmstead that antidiscrimination stat-
[L1178] utes “do[] not require” a covered entity “to alter” its services “simply to
[L1179] meet the reality that the handicapped have greater medical needs.” Id. In
[L1180] short, differential treatment based on bona fide medical needs is never
[L1181] discriminatory.
[L1182]    Even when patients with mental disabilities are arguably situated simi-
[L1183] larly to patients without such disabilities—because their needs could be
[L1184] addressed outside an institutional setting—other considerations may still
[L1185] justify treatment in an institution. 21 There are many reasons that anyone
[L1186] might be treated in an institutional setting—reasons that have nothing to
[L1187] do with mental disability. For example, institutional settings might be
[L1188] necessary to treat emergent conditions, Norfolk Cnty. Ret. Sys. v. Cmty.
[L1189] Health Sys., Inc., 877 F.3d 687, 690 (6th Cir. 2017), to ensure recovery
[L1190] after treatment for acute medical needs, United States ex rel. Gentry v.
[L1191] Encompass Health Rehab. Hosp. of Pearland, LLC, 157 F.4th 758, 761
[L1192] (5th Cir. 2025), or to treat chronic conditions associated with age, Fried-
[L1193] berg v. Schweiker, 721 F.2d 445, 448–49 (3d Cir. 1983). That individuals
[L1194] with mental disabilities are more likely to have needs that require treat-
[L1195] ment in a supervised setting than individuals without mental disabilities
[L1196] may necessitate “dissimilar treatment” compared to other individuals,
[L1197] Olmstead, 527 U.S. at 625 (Thomas, J., dissenting), but a state does not
[L1198] discriminate based on a protected characteristic merely because it “classi-
[L1199] fies on the basis of medical use” that correlates with that characteristic,
[L1200] Skrmetti, 145 S. Ct. at 1829.
[L1201]    It would be difficult to comprehensively list all the possible justifica-
[L1202] tions a state could raise for treating its mentally disabled patients in an
[L1203] in-patient setting—as the splintered Court learned when trying to write a

[L1215] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 28 / 39>[L1216]                        50 Op. O.L.C. __ (June 18, 2026)

[L1218] test in Olmstead. See supra Part I.B. But legitimate justifications could
[L1219] include concerns about the safety of the individual or the community.
[L1220] E.g., Foucha v. Louisiana, 504 U.S. 71, 80 (1992); Addington, 441 U.S. at
[L1221] 426. Such concerns go beyond the risk of violent behavior; they include
[L1222] the heightened risk that mentally disabled patients will be unable or
[L1223] unwilling to take necessary medication without the regular supervision
[L1224] that is only available in an institutional setting. See Natasha A. Spassiani
[L1225] et al., Did I Take My Medication Today? Understanding Medication Self-
[L1226] Management for Adults with Intellectual Disabilities Through Participa-
[L1227] tory Research, 38 J. Applied Rsch. Intell. Disabilities e70059, at 1–2
[L1228] (2025). Resource and space constraints in community-based treatment
[L1229] facilities must also be taken into account, lest the ADA be read in such a
[L1230] way as to “drive those in need of medical care and treatment . . . into
[L1231] settings with too little assistance and supervision.” Olmstead, 527 U.S. at
[L1232] 610 (Kennedy, J., concurring in the judgment).
[L1233]    Rather than attempting to provide an exhaustive list of proper justifica-
[L1234] tions, we conclude that institutional treatment constitutes disability dis-
[L1235] crimination only where the mere fact of disability—as opposed to the
[L1236] special needs resulting from that disability—is the sole factor motivating
[L1237] the choice of treatment setting. In other words, where the state has any
[L1238] nonarbitrary rationale for treating a disabled person in an institution, such
[L1239] treatment is not discriminatory under section 504 or Title II. Moreover,
[L1240] because the federal-state balance is at stake, supra Part II.A, state justifi-
[L1241] cations must be judged for rationality based on current realities—not
[L1242] “decades-old data and eradicated practices.” Shelby County, 570 U.S. at
[L1243] 551. Comparison to Title VII of the Civil Rights Act further supports this
[L1244] understanding. Title VII prohibits discrimination whenever a protected
[L1245] characteristic is “a motivating factor . . . , even [if] other factors also
[L1246] motivated the practice.” 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(m). Neither section 504 nor
[L1247] Title II contains such a provision, suggesting that disability discrimination
[L1248] is only prohibited when it is the sole motivating factor for treatment
[L1249] choices. Cf. San Francisco, 145 S. Ct. at 713–14.
[L1250]    Before committing a patient with mental disabilities to an institution—
[L1251] or upon request for a transfer by a patient currently institutionalized—
[L1252] states should assess the appropriateness and feasibility of both institution-
[L1253] al and community-based treatment options and make a decision based on
[L1254] a nonarbitrary rationale. What such rationales may be, however, present

[L1258] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 29 / 39>[L1259] Whether the Rehabilitation Act or ADA Impose or Authorize an Integration Mandate

[L1261] mixed questions of fact and policy that either are not answerable in the
[L1262] abstract or fall entirely outside the remit of this Office.

                                        3.

[L1266]    We have identified six potential counterarguments. None changes our
[L1267] conclusion. First, although our definition may be the more common one,
[L1268] at least one dictionary contemporary with the Rehabilitation Act defined
[L1269] “discrimination” more simply as “[a]n act based on prejudice.” The Amer-
[L1270] ican Heritage Dictionary of the English Language 376 (1971 ed.).
[L1271] “Most common English words have a number of dictionary definitions,
[L1272] some of them quite abstruse and rarely intended.” Antonin Scalia &
[L1273] Bryan A. Garner, Reading Law: The Interpretation of Legal Texts 70
[L1274] (2012); see also, e.g., Kasten v. Saint-Gobain Performance Plastics
[L1275] Corp., 563 U.S. 1, 7–8 (2011) (discussing different definitions of the verb
[L1276] “file”). Although some of their colleagues adopted a broader definition
[L1277] based on factors unique to the ADA (albeit not its text), 527 U.S. at 605–
[L1278] 06 (plurality opinion), four Justices in Olmstead agreed that the “ordinary
[L1279] interpretation and meaning of the term . . . discrimination” is that an
[L1280] individual “receive[s] differential treatment vis-à-vis members of a differ-
[L1281] ent group on the basis of a statutorily described characteristic,” id. at 611
[L1282] (Kennedy, J., concurring in the judgment) (quoting id. at 616 (Thomas, J.,
[L1283] dissenting, joined by Rehnquist, C.J., and Scalia, J.)). Even if the term
[L1284] encompassed prejudice more broadly, the statute would only prohibit
[L1285] institutional treatment that is based on “false and unjustified stereotypes.”
[L1286] Id. It would not mandate maximal integration in instances when institu-
[L1287] tional treatment is based on other factors.
[L1288]    Second, it could be argued that we are taking the term “discrimination”
[L1289] out of context. Both statutes also prohibit “exclud[ing]” from or
[L1290] “den[ying]” to disabled persons the benefits of services, programs, or
[L1291] activities offered by covered entities. 29 U.S.C. § 794(a); 42 U.S.C.
[L1292] § 12132. By their terms, however, the regulations imposing the integra-
[L1293] tion mandate aim to implement the statutes’ proscription on discrim-
[L1294] ination specifically, not these separate prohibitions. See 45 C.F.R.
[L1295] § 84.76(b); 28 C.F.R. § 35.130. HHS and DOJ cannot rely on alternative
[L1296] statutory bases to justify their rule. E.g., DHS v. Regents of the Univ. of
[L1297] Cal., 140 S. Ct. 1891, 1908–09 (2020); Citizens to Preserve Overton
[L1298] Park, Inc. v. Volpe, 401 U.S. 402, 420 (1971).

                                       29
[L1302] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 30 / 39>[L1303]                        50 Op. O.L.C. __ (June 18, 2026)

[L1305]    Even if HHS and DOJ were to try reframing their regulations, we do
[L1306] not think either agency could justify the integration mandate as imple-
[L1307] menting the prohibitions on exclusion and denial. To determine whether a
[L1308] right or benefit has been denied on a discriminatory basis, one must first
[L1309] identify the relevant right or benefit. In this instance, a clear majority of
[L1310] the Court agreed that the right or benefit is the medical “care and treat-
[L1311] ment of a large and diverse population of persons with mental disabili-
[L1312] ties.” Olmstead, 527 U.S. at 604 (plurality opinion); id. at 610 (Kennedy,
[L1313] J., concurring in the judgment); id. at 625–26 (Thomas, J., dissenting).
[L1314] The mandate does not affect the care that a mentally disabled individual
[L1315] receives—only the “setting” in which services are “administer[ed].” 45
[L1316] C.F.R. § 84.76(b); 28 C.F.R. § 35.130(d). In other words, an individual
[L1317] has not been denied or excluded from a service just because he receives it
[L1318] in a different setting. Cf. Tex. Democratic Party v. Abbott, 978 F.3d 168,
[L1319] 191 (5th Cir. 2020) (explaining that a person’s right is not abridged by “a
[L1320] law that makes it easier for others” to exercise that right).
[L1321]    Similar reasons preclude reliance on Congress’s expressed purpose of
[L1322] guaranteeing “equal opportunity” for disabled individuals. 29 U.S.C.
[L1323] § 701(b)(1)(F); see also 42 U.S.C. § 12101(a)(7). Although a legislative
[L1324] declaration of purpose is admittedly “an appropriate guide to the meaning
[L1325] of the statute’s operative provisions,” Gundy v. United States, 139 S. Ct.
[L1326] 2116, 2127 (2019) (cleaned up), a “general statement of purpose” cannot
[L1327] override the text of the operative provisions themselves, Sturgeon v.
[L1328] Frost, 587 U.S. 28, 55–56 (2019). To the extent Congress thought that
[L1329] integration was necessary to achieve its stated purposes, it clearly knew
[L1330] how to require it. See 42 U.S.C. § 12112(b)(1) (prohibiting disability-
[L1331] based segregation in employment); id. § 12182(b)(1)(B) (requiring public
[L1332] accommodations to provide “the most integrated setting appropriate” to
[L1333] disabled individuals). The omission of a comparable provision from
[L1334] Title II suggests that Congress did not consider maximal integration
[L1335] necessary to achieve “equal opportunity” in public services and programs
[L1336] for individuals with disabilities. 29 U.S.C. § 701(b)(1)(F). In any event,
[L1337] “congressional findings [are] a rather thin reed upon which to base a
[L1338] requirement . . . neither expressed nor . . . fairly implied in the operative
[L1339] sections of” the statutes. Nat’l Org. for Women, Inc. v. Scheidler, 510
[L1340] U.S. 249, 260 (1994).

                                     30
[L1344] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 31 / 39>[L1345] Whether the Rehabilitation Act or ADA Impose or Authorize an Integration Mandate

[L1347]    Third, it could be argued that the ban on “discrimination” in sec-
[L1348] tion 504 and Title II is sufficiently “broad” to encompass a generalized
[L1349] integration requirement. Of course, a statute may sometimes be “applied
[L1350] in situations not expressly anticipated by Congress” because of its
[L1351] “breadth.” Pa. Dep’t of Corr. v. Yeskey, 524 U.S. 206, 212 (1998) (cita-
[L1352] tion omitted). But such applications must still be consistent with the
[L1353] “single, best meaning” of the statute. Loper Bright Enters. v. Raimondo,
[L1354] 144 S. Ct. 2244, 2266 (2024). As we have explained, even if broad, the
[L1355] term “discrimination”—at least as used in section 504 and Title II—
[L1356] cannot be read to require maximal integration. Supra Part III.A.1.
[L1357]    Fourth, a critic will likely say that regardless of what the Marks nar-
[L1358] rowest-grounds rule dictates, our view depends on adopting the view of
[L1359] the concurrence or dissent in Olmstead, which by definition did not carry
[L1360] the day. Not so. We certainly agree with the dissent—and Justice Kenne-
[L1361] dy—that as a textual matter, discrimination under section 504 and Title II
[L1362] requires a showing that disabled individuals have been treated differently
[L1363] from similarly situated nondisabled persons. See Olmstead, 527 U.S. at
[L1364] 616 (Thomas, J., dissenting); id. at 611 (Kennedy, J., concurring in the
[L1365] judgment). As a result, if writing on a clean slate, we would not jettison
[L1366] the traditional meaning of discrimination for a “more comprehensive” one
[L1367] divorced from the text of the operative statutory provisions. Id. at 598
[L1368] (majority opinion). But our position is entirely consistent with the majori-
[L1369] ty’s holding that institutional isolation of individuals with mental disabili-
[L1370] ties can qualify as discrimination. We merely choose not to adopt the
[L1371] plurality’s expansive projection of the circumstances under which that
[L1372] might occur.
[L1373]    Fifth, it could be argued that regardless of what “discrimination” meant
[L1374] when the Rehabilitation Act and ADA were passed, Congress has now
[L1375] acquiesced in the “more comprehensive” view adopted by Olmstead by
[L1376] failing to amend the statutes. Id. But “[c]ongressional inaction cannot
[L1377] amend a duly enacted statute.” Patterson v. McLean Credit Union, 491
[L1378] U.S. 164, 175 n.1 (1989). The Supreme Court itself has explained that it is
[L1379] “‘impossible to assert with any degree of assurance that congressional
[L1380] failure to act represents’ affirmative congressional approval of the Court’s
[L1381] statutory interpretation.” Id. (citation omitted). In interpreting the relevant
[L1382] statutes, we therefore decline to take meaning from Congress’s silence
[L1383] in the wake of Olmstead. In any event, based on the narrowness of

                                       31
[L1387] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 32 / 39>[L1388]                        50 Op. O.L.C. __ (June 18, 2026)

[L1390] Olmstead’s holding, it is far from clear that Congress’s inaction—even if
[L1391] it were an implicit blessing of the Court’s decision—would cut against
[L1392] our conclusions here.
[L1393]     Sixth, the standard that we apply to assess whether institutionalization
[L1394] is justified could be criticized for rendering the ADA a nullity, since our
[L1395] test largely tracks the Fourteenth Amendment’s prohibition against disa-
[L1396] bility discrimination. See Cleburne Living Ctr., 473 U.S. at 439–40, 446.
[L1397] If it does so, that is because the Supreme Court told us to adopt this view:
[L1398] In Tennessee v. Lane, the Court explained that “Title II . . . seeks to en-
[L1399] force [the Fourteenth Amendment’s] prohibition on irrational disability
[L1400] discrimination.” 541 U.S. at 522 (emphasis added). Justice Kennedy
[L1401] echoed this point in Olmstead, saying that Title II “can be understood to
[L1402] deem as irrational, and so to prohibit” any distinction made “by reason of
[L1403] . . . disability and without adequate justification.” 527 U.S. at 611 (Ken-
[L1404] nedy, J., concurring in the judgment) (emphases added). Consistent with
[L1405] the source of Congress’s power to pass that statute, supra Part II.B.1,
[L1406] these statements reflect that Title II—and, by extension, section 504—
[L1407] forbids only institutional treatment that lacks rational justification.
[L1408]     Of course, evidence that a state’s justifications are pretextual will be
[L1409] relevant in deciding whether institutional treatment is, in fact, discrimina-
[L1410] tory in any given instance. Cf. McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411
[L1411] U.S. 792, 804–05 (1973). But the “ultimate burden” of proving discrimi-
[L1412] nation “remains at all times with the [complainant].” Ames v. Ohio Dep’t
[L1413] of Youth Servs., 145 S. Ct. 1540, 1545 n.2 (2025) (citation omitted).

                                     B.

[L1417]     Turning from the statute to the regulations that played so prominent a
[L1418] role in Olmstead, neither the reasoning nor the longevity of 45 C.F.R.
[L1419] § 84.76(b) and 28 C.F.R. § 35.130(d) persuades us that the foregoing
[L1420] textual analysis is incorrect. Although the Olmstead majority expressly
[L1421] disclaimed reliance on the now-defunct deference regime established in
[L1422] Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 467 U.S. 837 (1984),
[L1423] it nonetheless gave considerable deference to the views expressed in these
[L1424] regulations, see Olmstead, 527 U.S. at 597–98. As the Court recently
[L1425] emphasized, however, “[i]n the business of statutory interpretation, if [a
[L1426] reading of the text] is not the best, it is not permissible.” Loper Bright,
[L1427] 144 S. Ct. at 2266; cf. Interpretation of “Federal Means-Tested Public

                                     32
[L1431] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 33 / 39>[L1432] Whether the Rehabilitation Act or ADA Impose or Authorize an Integration Mandate

[L1434] Benefit” in the Personal Responsibility Work Opportunity Reconciliation
[L1435] Act of 1996, 49 Op. O.L.C. __, at *6 n.2 (Dec. 16, 2025) (noting the effect
[L1436] of Loper Bright both on court opinions and on those of this Office). At
[L1437] times, the best reading of a statute’s text can be that Congress has “con-
[L1438] fer[red] discretionary authority on agencies” to issue regulations based on
[L1439] their own understanding of what the statute requires. Loper Bright, 144
[L1440] S. Ct. at 2268. We conclude this is not such a time.

                                        1.

[L1444]    Section 504 requires each Executive Branch agency administering fed-
[L1445] eral financial assistance to “promulgate such regulations as may be neces-
[L1446] sary to carry out” the purposes of the section. 29 U.S.C. § 794(a). HHS’s
[L1447] predecessor—the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare
[L1448] (“HEW”)—was tasked with coordinating section 504 standards across
[L1449] federal agencies. See Exec. Order No. 11914 (1976). HEW included an
[L1450] early form of the integration mandate in 1977 when it promulgated regu-
[L1451] lations specific to programs to which HEW gave “federal financial assis-
[L1452] tance.” 42 Fed. Reg. 22,676 (May 4, 1977). A year later, HEW extended
[L1453] its own regulation to all federal agencies, creating the mandate as we
[L1454] know it today. See 43 Fed. Reg. 2,132 (Jan. 13, 1978).
[L1455]    When describing the statutory foundations of this regulation, HEW
[L1456] cited only “basic principles that [it] determined . . . to be inherent in
[L1457] section 504.” Id. at 2,134. Specifically, HEW read section 504’s “general
[L1458] prohibitions against discrimination on the basis of handicap” to include a
[L1459] guarantee of “equal opportunity and truly effective benefits and services”
[L1460] for disabled individuals. Id. On that basis, it invented the rule requiring
[L1461] that recipients of federal funds “administer programs and activities in the
[L1462] most integrated setting appropriate to the needs of qualified handicapped
[L1463] persons.” Id. at 2,138 (codified at 45 C.F.R. § 85.51(d) (1978)).
[L1464]    We are not persuaded by HEW’s analysis. As explained above, the
[L1465] “basic principles” of antidiscrimination upon which HEW purported to
[L1466] rely may be “inherent in section 504,” id. at 2,134, but they do not impose
[L1467] a mandate of maximal integration, supra Part III.A. We think that view is
[L1468] consistent not only with Olmstead but also with the sweep of the Supreme
[L1469] Court’s antidiscrimination jurisprudence. For example, the Court has
[L1470] repeatedly held that section 504 is concerned only with “evenhanded
[L1471] treatment,” not with “affirmative efforts to overcome the disabilities

                                       33
[L1475] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 34 / 39>[L1476]                         50 Op. O.L.C. __ (June 18, 2026)

[L1478] caused by handicaps.” Davis, 442 U.S. at 410. The same reasoning applies
[L1479] to the language in Title II, which runs parallel to section 504. Cf.
[L1480] Olmstead, 527 U.S. at 611 (Kennedy, J., concurring in the judgment); id.
[L1481] at 616 (Thomas, J., dissenting). Like the Court, we “decline to read into”
[L1482] these statutes a requirement that is “not to be found in the text” itself.
[L1483] Engine Mfrs. Ass’n v. S. Coast Air Quality Mgmt. Dist., 541 U.S. 246, 255
[L1484] (2004); accord Romag Fasteners, Inc. v. Fossil, Inc., 140 S. Ct. 1492,
[L1485] 1495 (2020) (declining to “read into statutes words that aren’t there”).

                                      2.

[L1489]    The Attorney General’s subsequent regulations fail for the same rea-
[L1490] sons. Indeed, following a statutory directive to make Title II regulations
[L1491] “consistent with . . . the coordination regulations . . . applicable to recipi-
[L1492] ents of Federal financial assistance under” section 504, the Attorney
[L1493] General issued a substantively identical rule with respect to Title II. See
[L1494] 56 Fed. Reg. at 35,719 (codified at 28 C.F.R. § 35.130(d)). In doing so,
[L1495] the Attorney General did not offer any independent legal analysis, refer-
[L1496] encing only HEW’s 1978 regulation and his perception that “Congress
[L1497] clearly intended the regulations issued under [T]itle II to adopt the stand-
[L1498] ards of section 504.” Id. at 35,703. As a result, the Attorney General’s
[L1499] analysis incorporates, rather than cures, any legal errors committed by
[L1500] HEW a decade earlier.
[L1501]    One potential counterargument to our conclusion that these regulations
[L1502] lack statutory support is that Title II’s instruction for the Attorney General
[L1503] to make regulations “consistent with” HEW’s 1978 coordinating regula-
[L1504] tions ratified the integration mandate. 42 U.S.C. § 12134(b). We are
[L1505] unpersuaded. “Absent . . . overwhelming evidence of [congressional]
[L1506] acquiescence,” it is always a risky business to “replace the plain text and
[L1507] original understanding of a statute with an . . . agency interpretation.”
[L1508] Solid Waste Agency of N. Cook Cnty. v. U.S. Army Corps of Eng’rs, 531
[L1509] U.S. 159, 170 n.5 (2001) (“SWANCC”). Here, Title II does not approve
[L1510] the substance of the regulations either by “statutory incorporation,” Motor
[L1511] Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n of the U.S., Inc. v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co.,
[L1512] 463 U.S. 29, 45 (1983), or by “express[] ratifi[cation],” Zuber v. Allen,
[L1513] 396 U.S. 168, 194 n.30 (1969) (citation omitted). Rather, the statute
[L1514] reflects Congress’s desire for regulatory consistency in implementing the
[L1515] Rehabilitation Act and the ADA—hardly “overwhelming evidence” of

                                      34
[L1519] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 35 / 39>[L1520] Whether the Rehabilitation Act or ADA Impose or Authorize an Integration Mandate

[L1522] Congress’s acquiescence to the integration mandate specifically.
[L1523] SWANCC, 531 U.S. at 169–70 n.5.22 In 2012, then-Judge Gorsuch drew
[L1524] this very conclusion, explaining that “[s]ection 12134(b) does not incor-
[L1525] porate the Rehabilitation Act’s regulations into the ADA or direct the
[L1526] Attorney General to promulgate identical regulations for Title II.” Elwell
[L1527] v. Oklahoma ex rel. Bd. of Regents of the Univ. of Okla., 693 F.3d 1303,
[L1528] 1313 (10th Cir. 2012). “It simply says the Attorney General’s regulations
[L1529] must be ‘consistent’—that is, compatible or not contradictory—with those
[L1530] under the Rehabilitation Act.” Id.
[L1531]    Indeed, during the Chevron era, “even an unequivocal ratification” of
[L1532] the integration mandate “would not connote approval or disapproval of an
[L1533] agency’s later decision to rescind the regulation.” State Farm, 463 U.S. at
[L1534] 45. After all, at the time, if Congress approved the agency’s interpreta-
[L1535] tion, it would only have been as a reasonable policy choice under the
[L1536] terms of the existing statute—“even if the agency’s reading differs from
[L1537] what [a] court believes is the best statutory interpretation.” Nat’l Cable &
[L1538] Telecomms. Ass’n v. Brand X Internet Servs., 545 U.S. 967, 980 (2005).
[L1539] Under that framework, it is far from clear whether any particular member
[L1540] of Congress—let alone Congress as a whole—would have understood the
[L1541] regulation to which he supposedly acquiesced as representing the best
[L1542] interpretation of the statute in question. As a result, even if the consisten-
[L1543] cy provision in section 12134 could be seen as ratifying the 1978 HEW
[L1544] regulations as a reasonable interpretation of section 504, it would not fix
[L1545] those regulations as the best interpretation of Title II. HHS and DOJ can
[L1546] thus rescind their integration-mandate regulations because Title II does
[L1547] not, by its terms, mandate maximal integration. 23

[L1549]    22 Congress also forbade construing the ADA “to apply a lesser standard than the

[L1551] standards applied under . . . the Rehabilitation Act . . . or the regulations issued by Federal

[L1553] Congress meant the ADA to be as protective of disabled individuals as the Rehabilitation
[L1554] Act. It does not fix the substantive standards for implementing either statute.

[L1566] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 36 / 39>[L1567]                            50 Op. O.L.C. __ (June 18, 2026)

[L1569]    Related to—though analytically distinct from—ratification, we
[L1570] acknowledge that the best argument in favor of the integration mandate is
[L1571] its longevity. Like the Supreme Court, we think that “the informed judg-
[L1572] ment” of Executive Branch entities entrusted with administering a statute
[L1573] “could be entitled to ‘great weight,’” especially when reflected in “an
[L1574] interpretation issued contemporaneously with the enactment of the [rele-
[L1575] vant] statute.” Loper Bright, 144 S. Ct. at 2259 (citation omitted). But
[L1576] even longstanding interpretations have, at most, the “power to persuade,”
[L1577] dependent on “the thoroughness evident in [the agency’s] consideration,
[L1578] the validity of its reasoning, [and] its consistency with earlier and later
[L1579] pronouncements.” Id. (citation omitted). For reasons already explained,
[L1580] HEW’s reasoning is not persuasive, and the Attorney General’s reasoning
[L1581] is effectively nonexistent. What is more, HEW’s original view, which was
[L1582] based on “the plain language of the [Rehabilitation] Act,” Davis, 442 U.S.
[L1583] at 404 n.4, was that “Congress had not intended any regulations to be
[L1584] issued” for the implementation of section 504, id. at 411–12 n.11. HEW
[L1585] imposed the integration mandate only after reversing that position, which
[L1586] “substantially diminishes the deference to be given to HEW’s . . . inter-
[L1587] pretation of the statute.” Id.; see also, e.g., Chamber of Com. of the U.S. v.
[L1588] U.S. Dep’t of Lab., 885 F.3d 360, 381 (5th Cir. 2018).

                                           3.

[L1592]    Nor do we consider “the best reading” of section 504 and Title II to be
[L1593] that either statute “delegates discretionary authority” to impose such a
[L1594] mandate. Loper Bright, 144 S. Ct. at 2263. As a result, we conclude that
[L1595] 45 C.F.R. § 84.76(b) and 28 C.F.R. § 35.130(d) exceed the scope of
[L1596] authority granted to HHS and DOJ to implement the statutory proscrip-
[L1597] tions on disability-based discrimination.
[L1598]    “[R]egulations, in order to be valid, must be consistent with the statute
[L1599] under which they are promulgated.” Decker, 568 U.S. at 609 (citation
[L1600] omitted). Because antidiscrimination statutes authorize only that which is

[L1602] state-provided, community-based services. Id. The legality of that guidance is beyond the
[L1603] scope of this opinion. Given that such guidance goes further than even DOJ’s prior
[L1604] interpretation, which we now conclude to have been overbroad, however, it too must fall.
[L1605] Moreover, we emphasize that, by definition, guidance documents “do not have the force
[L1606] and effect of law.” Perez v. Mortgage Bankers Ass’n, 575 U.S. 92, 97 (2015) (quoting
[L1607] Shalala v. Guernsey Mem’l Hosp., 514 U.S. 87, 99 (1995)).

                                          36
[L1611] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 37 / 39>[L1612] Whether the Rehabilitation Act or ADA Impose or Authorize an Integration Mandate

[L1614] “necessary to eliminate discrimination,” Davis, 442 U.S. at 410, the
[L1615] Supreme Court has already held that section 504 does not authorize regu-
[L1616] lations imposing “affirmative-action obligation[s]” on federal-funding
[L1617] recipients to “accommodat[e] . . . the needs of handicapped individuals,”
[L1618] id. at 411. In doing so, the Court rejected the argument that section 504
[L1619] “impose[d] an obligation to ensure full participation in covered programs
[L1620] by handicapped individuals and . . . to make the kind of adjustments that
[L1621] would be necessary to permit [their] safe participation in the . . . pro-
[L1622] gram.” Id. at 409. Regulations that created such requirements, the Court
[L1623] explained, constituted “an unauthorized extension of the obligations
[L1624] imposed by th[e] statute,” which the implementing agency “lack[ed] the
[L1625] authority” to impose. Id. at 410, 412.
[L1626]    The text of section 504 makes this limit on regulatory authority clear. It
[L1627] authorizes only “such regulations as may be necessary to carry out” the
[L1628] statute’s antidiscrimination provision. 29 U.S.C. § 794(a) (emphasis
[L1629] added). This is a tighter nexus than many other statutes empowering
[L1630] agencies to create regulations. 24 Under its ordinary meaning, to be “neces-
[L1631] sary,” a regulation must be “something that is logically required or logi-
[L1632] cally inevitable.” Webster’s Third New International at 1510; see also,
[L1633] e.g., Random House at 955 (“being essential, indispensable, or requisite”).
[L1634] We share the Supreme Court’s longstanding view that “affirmative efforts
[L1635] to overcome the disabilities caused by handicaps” are not logically re-
[L1636] quired to eliminate discrimination. Davis, 442 U.S. at 410; cf. Barr, 140
[L1637] S. Ct. at 2354 (noting that “cur[ing] . . . unequal treatment” does not
[L1638] necessarily require “extending the benefits or burdens to the exempted
[L1639] class”). Indeed, the HHS regulation goes further even than Olmstead’s
[L1640] plurality by requiring states to transfer a patient to a more integrated
[L1641] setting, if available, even when the patient consents to institutional treat-
[L1642] ment. See OLP Memo at 6–7. Because institutional treatment does not
[L1643] amount to discrimination merely if there is a more integrated setting
[L1644] available, generally mandating maximal integration is not “necessary to
[L1645] carry out” section 504. 29 U.S.C. § 794(a). Consequently, 45 C.F.R.
[L1646] § 84.76(b) exceeds HHS’s authority under the statute.
[L1647]    The question of DOJ’s authority under Title II is somewhat closer, but
[L1648] the same principles lead us to the same conclusion. Title II requires the

[L1650]    24 See, e.g., 12 U.S.C. § 5512(b)(1); 21 U.S.C. § 371(a); 29 U.S.C. §§ 652(8), 655(b);

[L1652] 42 U.S.C. § 1382i; 46 U.S.C. § 70003(e).

                                          37
[L1656] <PARSED TEXT FOR PAGE: 38 / 39>[L1657]                            50 Op. O.L.C. __ (June 18, 2026)

[L1659] Attorney General to issue regulations “consistent with this chapter
[L1660] and with the coordination regulations” under section 504. 42 U.S.C.
[L1661] § 12134(b). Although not necessary to eliminate discrimination, the
[L1662] integration mandate could arguably be considered consistent with that
[L1663] goal in that it simply raises the standard of inclusivity above the floor set
[L1664] by Title II. Cf. Guardians Ass’n v. Civ. Serv. Comm’n of the City of New
[L1665] York, 463 U.S. 582, 635, 643 (1983) (Stevens, J., dissenting) (concluding
[L1666] “an administrative agency may validly impose additional requirements”
[L1667] that are “consistent with . . . [statutory] objectives”). But it could also be
[L1668] said that “permit[ting] agencies to proscribe conduct that Congress did not
[L1669] intend to prohibit” would be “inconsistent with” a limited statutory prohi-
[L1670] bition. Id. at 615 (O’Connor, J., concurring in the judgment).
[L1671]    We believe that the latter view comports more with Title II. Congress
[L1672] intentionally chose not to require general and maximal integration of
[L1673] mentally disabled patients served by states and other public entities. Supra
[L1674] Part III.A.1. Title II, like section 504, aims only to ensure “the evenhand-
[L1675] ed treatment of qualified handicapped persons” vis-à-vis their nondisabled
[L1676] peers. Davis, 442 U.S. at 410. Because “the expressed will of Congress is
[L1677] that [public entities] are prohibited only from . . . discriminating” based
[L1678] on disability, we conclude that a regulation proscribing nondiscriminatory
[L1679] action is inconsistent with Title II. Guardians Ass’n, 463 U.S. at 615
[L1680] (O’Connor, J., concurring in the judgment). 25
[L1681]    We acknowledge that this position contravenes the longstanding prac-
[L1682] tice of both HHS and CRT. For the reasons already explained, we hold the
[L1683] reasoning undergirding the agencies’ earlier practice is inconsistent with
[L1684] the “single, best meaning” of section 504 and Title II. Loper Bright, 144
[L1685] S. Ct. at 2266.

[L1689]   For the reasons discussed above, we conclude that notwithstanding the
[L1690] broad interpretation many courts and commentators have given Olmstead,

[L1692]     25 A House committee report on Title II stated that part of the intended purpose of Ti-

[L1694] tle II was to “direct the Attorney General to issue regulations setting forth the forms of

[L1696] statement were law (and it is not), it would establish, at most, that Congress gave the

[L1708] basis of disability as that term is used in section 504 of the Rehabilitation
[L1709] Act and Title II of the ADA. If, in passing those proscriptions, Congress
[L1710] had imposed an integration mandate on state and local governments, both
[L1711] statutes would raise grave constitutional concerns. However, we need not
[L1712] resolve that issue here, because Congress did not purport to impose such a
[L1713] mandate, nor did it authorize HHS or DOJ to do so.

**Now this is evidence of a policy-to-operation chain that the previous assessments missed.**

Your 39-page document is a June 18, 2026, opinion from the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel, written in response to a February 17 request from White House Counsel. It argues that the ADA and Rehabilitation Act do not require states to provide treatment in the most integrated setting appropriate to people with mental disabilities. <FileCite ref="turn9file0" line_range_start={4} line_range_end={21}/><FileCite ref="turn9file0" line_range_start={100} line_range_end={137}/>

The consequential passage is on page 28. The opinion proposes that institutionalization need not be considered discriminatory whenever the state has a nonarbitrary rationale for it. That substantially changes the legal position the federal government is preparing to defend.

And page 35 goes further: **the opinion recommends rescinding federal guidance supporting community integration.** <FileCite ref="turn9file0" line_range_start={1218} line_range_end={1255}/><FileCite ref="turn9file0" line_range_start={1544} line_range_end={1562}/>

This is not a detention order. It is a documented effort to remove an obstacle to institutionalization. The important question is whether that effort has progressed into government action.

## The implementation is already underway

This is the sequence established by independent public records:

| Date | Documented action |
|---|---|
| **July 24, 2025** | Executive Order 14321 directed federal agencies to encourage civil commitment, pursue removal of judicial and consent-decree barriers, and prioritize certain state and local programs that use institutional treatment. <Cite ref="turn329309search4"/> |
| **June 18, 2026** | DOJ issued the legal opinion you uploaded, challenging the community-integration mandate. <Cite ref="turn329309search0"/> |
| **July 20, 2026** | DOJ published notice that it would stop relying on longstanding *Olmstead* enforcement guidance. <Cite ref="turn889215view6"/> |
| **September 23, 2026** | A federal court approved the government's request to remove the community-integration provisions from HHS's 2024 Section 504 regulations, with nationwide effect. <Cite refs={["turn329309search11","turn329309search8"]}/> |

**That is no longer merely an ideological proposal.** It is a sequence of presidential direction, legal reinterpretation, enforcement withdrawal, and regulatory rollback.

## Rebuilt assessment: the critical finding

**The government has already established a nationwide domestic military response capability. The unresolved question is whether, when, and under whose authority it will be activated for civilian operations.**

That conclusion rests on three primary records:

1. **Executive Order 14339, August 25, 2025:** Directs the availability of a standing National Guard quick-reaction capability for nationwide deployment. <Cite ref="turn962988view2"/>
2. **National Guard Bureau implementation memorandum, October 31, 2025:** Requires state and territorial response forces to be operational by April 1, 2026, with approximately 25% deployable within eight hours and the full force within 24 hours. That is a readiness requirement, not evidence of an activation order. <Cite ref="turn962988view0"/>
3. **Congressional inquiry, October 23, 2026:** Senators Kelly and Slotkin specifically demanded the missing information: command authority, activation triggers, contemplated DHS/DOJ support, and deployment plans. The requested response deadline was October 28. <Cite ref="turn962988view3"/>

**An important correction:** The National Guard Response Force and the separate nationwide Quick Reaction Force must not be conflated. Their readiness, command structures, and legal authorities require separate scrutiny.

The report will treat military preparation as a **leading indicator**, distinguish it from actual deployment, and assess what additional developments would indicate a threat to civilians.

In 2026 the Section 1557, Title IX, and Medicaid/CHIP records show real administrative actions; they do not, by themselves, prove a covert lethal plan. [R16–R21, R27]

**Bottom line:** The conditions for additional coercive encounters already exist. A coordinated, nationwide transfer of civilian policing to the military is **not established** by the records reviewed. The warning system below tests for *orders, mission changes, and operational effects*, rather than requiring a public proclamation or waiting for deaths.

## 1 · What has actually changed in 2026

Another correction: the NGQRF memo says operational **January 1, 2026**, not April. Do not substitute assertions about unit readiness for actual October 2026 readiness returns. [R01, R02, R26]

| P02 | Some encounters will create **additional civilian safety hazards**; precise timing and victims are indeterminate | **Plausible; unquantified**. More encounters increase exposure, but available data do not yield a validated per-encounter injury probability [R06–R10] | Comparable high-volume operations with verified low force/injury rates would reduce concern |

Readiness mechanism exists; active mission orders not obtained; legal constraints strengthened [R01–R04] | Verified new Guard taskings would strengthen; confirmed nonactivation and mission restrictions would weaken |
| P04 | Patient access or medical response **may** be obstructed when federal operations and protests intersect | **Credible hazard, low timing confidence**. Severe consequence warrants monitoring, not a manufactured date | Independently confirmed command transfers, deployment orders and displacement of civilian governance across multiple states |

*Confidence is qualitative analytic judgment, not a calibrated probability or a rating of political actors. P02 and P04 are conditional exposure forecasts, not assertions of an impending targeted attack.*

## 3 · The three operational chains that matter

### A. From civilian enforcement capacity to field exposure

**Signed agreements → recruitment/contracts → written field tasking → deployed officers → stop/detention operations → potential civilian contact → recorded use of force → investigation.**

An early warning must be sought at **field tasking and deployment**, not at the last two steps. The October 31 Reuters email describing an existing Central Valley operation is closer to that threshold than a later injury tally. A 287(g) memorandum is only evidence of delegated authority; it cannot be silently converted into an actual deployment, officer count, use-of-force incident, or death. [R05–R08]

**Measured footprint:** ICE's published roster stood at **2,466 agreements on September 8**, **2,654 on October 9**, and **2,725 on October 30**. That is **259 additional active memorandums (10.5%) over 52 days**, according to successive published snapshots. Signings are not linear predictors of arrests and do not show how many officers are actively operating. [R05]

**Next useful signal:** A dated new regional mission directive, internal notification corroborated by local observation, or change in agents' legal responsibilities. A social post alleging activity without origin, time, or corroboration does not meet this threshold.

### B. From Guard readiness to civilian military functions

**Readiness requirement → actual unit status → mission assignment → legal authority and command → mobilization → civilian policing function → effects on rights and treatment access.**

The 2025 NGQRF implementation memo directs an HRF/CASE mission set of **200 personnel**, with 25% prepared within 8 hours, 50% within 12 and 100% within 24, and monthly readiness reports. This is **not** evidence of an order to mobilize this week. [R01]

The National Guard Reaction Force (NGRF) is a **separate, existing** state/territorial force, ordinarily under home-state command. Its public fact sheet describes site security, roadblocks, civil-disturbance control and critical-infrastructure protection, with initial personnel response within eight hours. The distinct NGQRF and NGRF structures must not be conflated into one uniform national force. [R23]

The **2026 command gap** is defined in the signed October 23 Senate letter: who commands, which status applies (Title 10, Title 32, State Active Duty, or dual-status), whether forces could support DHS/DOJ, what triggers mission assignment, and what notice goes to Congress. The letter's **October 29** deadline passed without a corresponding public response located in this review. [R02]

**Counterweight:** On October 23 the Ninth Circuit affirmed a preliminary injunction against the initial 2025 California federalization order. The court's reasoning constrains one path under **10 U.S.C. §12406**; it does not ban all Guard assistance under every state or federal authority. U.S. Northern Command separately reports early-2026 demobilization in Los Angeles, Chicago and Portland and the March release of Texas standby troops. These are meaningful disconfirming facts for claims of uninterrupted federalized military occupation in those cities. [R03, R24]

**Next useful signal:** Signed or contemporaneously verified activation instructions stating which force, which governor/federal command, which law, what civilian function and where. Observe the distinction between protecting a federal building and assuming police powers over the surrounding public. No source establishes a specific synchronized future nationwide order.

### C. From policy blueprint to real-world health exposure

**Advocacy recommendation → executive/agency decision → published rule → judicial review → state/payer implementation → care interruption → patient outcome.**

The original *Mandate for Leadership* proposed changes to Section 1557 enforcement. In June 2026, HHS announced that a court had vacated **specific** provisions of the 2024 nondiscrimination rule involving gender-identity discrimination; HHS emphasized that other protections continue. The Education Department's September 29 rule recodified the 2020 Title IX text following judicial vacatur of the 2024 rule. Neither event means every federal civil-rights statute was repealed. [R18–R20]

A separate CMS rule restricting federal Medicaid/CHIP payment for certain gender-affirming procedures for minors took effect **October 13** and includes transition provisions for specified existing hormone treatment. Michigan issued a provider bulletin **November 2** to implement related claims policy. This is a policy-to-operations chain with immediate impacts on payment and authorization, **not** evidence that all clinical treatment is illegal or that a particular patient has been harmed. [R16–R17, R27]

The April 30 DOJ report implementing the anti-Christian-bias task force illustrates another proposal-to-action path. Whether its substantive allegations are supported is a separate evidentiary question; creating the task force and issuing a report are verified acts. [R21]

**Next useful signal:** Specific claim denials, provider notices, treatment interruptions, litigation stays, and actual clinical consequences—not ideological summaries.

## 4 · Civilian medical response: the institutional hazard

The prior attacks on identifiable medical volunteers at Broadview, Illinois, and the cross-city Physicians for Human Rights dataset establish that force can reach people providing care. They do not identify a future target or date. The January killing of an ICU nurse similarly shows that a civilian's profession does not protect them from lethal violence, but it cannot establish that the shooting occurred *because he was a nurse*. [R09–R10]

**Clinical exposure pathway:** civilians injured in an operation → an unprotected treatment location or interrupted ambulance access → delay, second exposure, lost patient access, or inability to complete care. This is a failure of the environment, command and use-of-force control—not a tactical failure by a medic already working on a patient.

**What changes the assessment before a death:** verified interference with emergency dispatch, repeated chemical-agent use near medical areas, blocked ambulances, orders limiting treatment access, or credible advance notice of a large armed operation near an operating clinic or shelter. No verified November 2026 nationwide order to attack medical responders was identified.

**Institution-level options:** Health systems and EMS leadership can arrange clear law-enforcement liaison and escalation contacts, document protected transport access, build independent incident capture, and require prompt reporting of interference. Individual clinicians cannot make an unexpected shooting safe through better scene prediction. These are general continuity measures, not instructions for confrontation.

## 5 · Coupled systems: water, healthcare and public safety

The July 30 FBI/EPA notice states that water-sector facilities in at least **seven states** reported cyber incidents beginning July 27, with some operational degradation. CISA separately reports PLC disruptions that forced some operators into manual operations and caused boil-water notices. The exposure is real and geographically distributed, but the agencies do **not** provide a named November attack site or a timetable for a national water outage. [R14–R15]

The actionable chain is **loss of utility control → degraded service/water advisories → increased burden on healthcare and emergency response**. The relevant warning signs for residents and care facilities are utility-issued advisories, sustained operating failures, and emergency-management notices—not attribution claims about who is behind an outage.

A concurrent regional infrastructure disruption plus armed intervention might increase stress on responders. **Coincidence is not coordination.** A common perpetrator requires linked technical telemetry, shared command/tasking evidence, or another independent bridge between events. No such chain was established here.

## 6 · Where exposure could plausibly change

**West Coast:** The strongest contemporary operational receipt is the **October California Central Valley enforcement surge**. The October 23 Ninth Circuit ruling is a legal counterweight to California Guard federalization under the challenged statute. Neither finding establishes an imminent threat to an individual West Coast child or a statewide military action. [R03, R06]

**Texas:** Federal-local enforcement partnerships and detention infrastructure are material factors. GAO's September 2026 detention expansion report identifies planning failures at the system level; it cannot identify a particular Texas county's next fatal incident. The March 2026 NORTHCOM standby-release statement also prevents the inference that old federalized troop arrangements remain active in every earlier staging location. [R05, R13, R24]

**Washington, DC and Memphis:** These are jurisdictions with separately documented Guard involvement in civilian security. NPR reported D.C. Marshals deputization with limited authority to detain, not to make arrests. Prosecutors' **November** release of Memphis footage concerned a **July** fatality and factual disputes; it is not a new shooting this week. They are examples of the military–civilian interface actually being exercised, not proof that it has become a national martial-law system. [R22, R25]

**Water utilities nationally:** A specific town can be at risk even if national incident numbers remain modest. The July federal notices establish a real hazard but do not establish a particular threat to a Texas, California, Oregon or Washington utility during this forecast window. [R14–R15]

## 7 · Decision windows and warning thresholds

| Window | Watch for | Evidence standard | Civilian / institutional decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Now–72 hours** | Fresh written enforcement deployments; Guard activation announcements or independently corroborated orders; utilities issuing emergency advisories | Dated agency document **or** independent credible confirmations of field effects | Prefer direct local incident, utility, and emergency notices over rumors; maintain normal services absent a locality-specific trigger |
| **Days 4–14** | Sustained regional operational expansion; formal cross-agency assignments; court action changing legal authority; new payer denials | Two independent records or a controlling dated order | Review access-to-care and emergency response arrangements in affected jurisdictions |
| **Days 15–30** | Repeated use-of-force patterns; persistent access obstruction; multiple utilities affected by a confirmed common cause; command and governance displacement | Documented repeating events plus a tested linkage | Escalate institutional reporting, independent oversight requests, and targeted protective measures |
| **Any time** | Direct threat to a named person or facility; live violence; urgent water contamination advisory | Specific, credible, time- and place-grounded alert | Follow local emergency instructions, seek safety and emergency services as warranted; do not wait for this report to update |

**High-consequence warning that would change the model:** confirmed simultaneous commands across multiple jurisdictions assigning military personnel ordinary civilian arrest, search, detention or movement-control responsibilities **plus** evidence of enforcement over civilian institutions. That combination warrants an immediate reassessment; neither military readiness alone nor a provocative speech is enough.

**Action for a medical response institution:** Ask whether the jurisdiction's emergency operations plans contain an independently documented mechanism for clearing patient access, reporting impeded care, and investigating force against medics. A report that merely records a medic's eventual injury is too late to be a warning.

## 8 · Alternative explanations and falsification

- **H1 — Large-scale routine enforcement rather than a new military intervention.** Supported by ICE agreements and October operation reporting. Weakened by verified formal military assignments to ordinary civilian policing; strengthened by sustained operations without new Guard orders. [R05–R08]
- **H2 — Localized force escalation associated with operational tempo.** Possible, but quantitative predictions of injuries or deaths are unsupported by available denominators. Weakened by documented reductions in force per comparable encounter; strengthened by independently confirmed repeat harm in newly activated operations. [R09–R11]
- **H3 — Expanding military control over ordinary civilian functions.** Serious contingency. Needs activation documents, legal-command chain and actual civilian functions. Judicial constraints and demobilizations prevent treating the pathway as already completed nationally. [R01–R04, R24]
- **H4 — Multiple independent utility incidents.** Supported by FBI/EPA and CISA 2026 alerts; not proof of common direction with enforcement operations. Correlation becomes a coordinated-action finding only with shared technical, operational or communicative evidence. [R14–R15]
- **H5 — Project 2025 policy implementation predicts later harms automatically.** This is not a valid causal shortcut. Policy-to-action chains are real in several sectors; outcomes require state implementation, court status, claims and actual patient-level evidence. [R16–R21]
- **H6 — A single hidden national operation explains every violent event, utility incident and medical disruption.** Not currently demonstrated. Test by identifying a common authority, instruction, schedule, resourcing chain or independently authenticated operational linkage; reject causal inference from timing alone.

## 10 · Missing records that would materially change the answer

1. **October 20, 2026 NGQRF readiness returns** for personnel, equipment and training. The 2025 signed memo requires these reports; this assessment did not obtain the 2026 returns. [R01]
2. **Response, if any, to the signed October 23 Senate inquiry due October 29**, addressing current command, mobilization, guard-governor relationships and support to DHS/DOJ. A publicly released response was not located; that does not mean no internal response exists. [R02]
3. **Dated field deployment/tasking records** for the California regional surge, comparable operations elsewhere, and agency changes that increase civilian exposure. Reuters reviewed an internal email; this assessment does not possess a complete national tasking list. [R06]
4. **Encounter-denominated force data** and body-camera activation/compliance by location and mission. GAO describes mechanisms missing from existing oversight. [R11]
5. **Local operational status and advisories for water systems.** Federal alerts cover a multi-state pattern but do not identify currently affected Texas or West Coast customers. [R14–R15]
6. **Actual payer denials and provider notices after Oct 13** to determine whether coverage rules result in treatment interruptions; do not claim clinical deaths from rule text alone. [R16–R17]

## 11 · Analytic method and boundaries

This is a forward assessment based on **dated public documents and independently reported operational acts**. It is not covert-source collection, an intelligence bulletin, or evidence of access to classified deployment orders. This distinction is particularly important when the user's actual question is *what happens next* rather than *who died already*.

Evidence labels: **Verified** = direct court/agency instrument; **Reported** = professional journalism with stated sourcing; **Calculated** = transparent arithmetic applied to source figures; **Unresolved** = missing, contested or non-public evidence. Trends are mapped across decisions and their implementation; a policy proposal alone is not proof of implementation or causation. The attached Project 2025 screenshot from the prior discussion was **not** treated as proof of governmental action. The original Heritage publication and later agency documents were checked independently.

The selected 30-day window is an **assessment horizon**, not a mathematically inferred date. It does not support invented probabilities, exact targets, forced causal links, or a guarantee of safety. Earlier medical and mortality events are used as established **failure modes**, never substituted for contemporary leading indicators. Evidence of judicial resistance, demobilization and limited Pentagon assurances is retained even though it complicates the escalation hypothesis.

**Decision rule:** If a new dated, authenticated order changes command authority or authorizes military participation in civilian enforcement; if operational interference with care is independently confirmed; or if a local critical-infrastructure advisory identifies immediate danger, the assessment must change **on that evidence**, without waiting for new deaths or a formal proclamation.
